  • Open. Every rank then calls open with its rank and the attempt. It raises ValueError naming the differing keys if the stored manifest differs, and loads the recorded progress.
  • Logs. Each rank appends to its own log, named by attempt and rank. mark_done appends a line and fsyncs; torn or unparseable lines are skipped. path must be shared by all ranks.
  • Listed once. Only rank 0 calls remaining; Pipeline broadcasts it.

Pipeline builds the manifest as JSON: version (2), streams (per stream: dims, non-spatial labels, grid ID and dtype, and whether it is written), seed (runner.seed or null), member_groups (the distinct ordered member groups of the items, [[]] without members), and tags. The store merges its tags in, so a tag change is a mismatch. Model identity is not detectable, so callers record it in tags, such as the model name and checkpoint; a resume that skips items from a store without tags logs a warning.

Progress and stores are cleared independently: overwriting a store but not its progress skips items whose data is gone.

docs.title: Distribution
docs.text:
def distribute_work(items: Sequence[T], rank: int, world_size: int) -> list[T]: ...
def rank_info() -> tuple[int, int]: ...  # (rank, world_size); (0, 1) if uninitialized
def rank0_first(fn: Callable[[], T]) -> T: ...  # rank 0 runs fn, barrier, then the rest
def broadcast(obj: T | None) -> T: ...  # rank 0's object on every rank
def barrier() -> None: ...
def raise_if_any_failed(error: Exception | None) -> None: ...  # all ranks agree

Each rank gets one contiguous, balanced slice; idle ranks get []. Helpers call torch.distributed directly and are no-ops without a process group. Core never initializes one: launch with torchrun and call init_process_group, or use physicsnemo's DistributedManager, which is optional.

docs.title: Built-in runners
docs.text:
PrognosticRunner(prognostic, source=None, forcing=None, diagnostics=None, seed=0, source_member=None, perturbation=None) drives create_iterator and publishes the initial condition as the first step, matching run.deterministic, when the input ends at zero and the output declares every input variable on the input's grid; otherwise the streams start at the first forecast. The published initial condition holds only the input variables. When the output declares more (diagnostic outputs such as tp06), the forecast store holds NaN for those variables at lead time 0. Pipeline keeps the selected output_variables each output holds and skips an output holding none of them, so neither the scorer nor the store sees it and the store keeps its fill value. A diagnostic stream whose inputs include output-only variables starts at the first forecast. Each step advances by the model's step interval (see E2S-06_MODEL_CONTRACT_SPEC.md). Sources default to default_sources(). Declared forcing is fetched initially and its time-varying slots are sent every step. The prognostic stream is forecast; each diagnostic adds a stream under the caller's name.

DiagnosticRunner(diagnostics, source=None, step=None, seed=0, source_member=None) applies diagnostics directly to source data. Step k fetches inputs at the item's time plus k * step; without step, an item is one step at lead time zero.

PrognosticRunner and DiagnosticRunner support single-slot models only: a prognostic or diagnostic whose input_coords() returns a tuple of slots raises ValueError at construction. Run multi-slot models as components of the coupled runner.

Every runner fits fetched data to a model with map_field, which selects and never regrids. It raises ValueError when a source does not cover the target's range on a numeric axis (a label more than one source spacing beyond it). It does not check resolution: a source coarser than the target is selected by nearest label and repeats neighbouring values. Fetch such sources with fetch_data(target_grid=...) or RegriddedSource.

The coupled runner, earth2studio.coupling.CoupledRunner, lives with the coupler (E2S-12_COUPLING_SPEC.md). Per item it fetches each component's initial condition from bound sources, runs components at their own cadences, and yields component-named streams.

All three batch members (supports_member_batching = True) and take source_member (see Source members above).

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
Rule Requirement X1 output_coords gives one signature per stream; time/ensemble are never fixed X2 Stream signatures carry the yielded fields' grid metadata and auxiliary coordinates X3 Outputs have dims time (item.time only), then the schema's fixed dims X4 Output lead_time labels lie within the schema's; other fixed labels equal it X5 Each item seeds stochastic models once, from its first member's member_seed X6 Perturbations draw each member alone from its member_seed (base seed, time, member) X7 Every rank passes identical items, or run raises ValueError first X8 Stores are planned from all items, so resume at any world size reuses them X9 distribute_work slices evenly and contiguously; idle ranks join collectives X10 Per-stream mappings raise ValueError for unknown stream names X11 A regridder's source_grid must match its stream, or run raises first X12 Streams absent from output are not written; run logs them once X13 Rank 0 creates stores before other ranks prepare them; re-adding is a no-op (I4) X14 Distributed stores write blocks of 1 along time and ensemble X15 Distributed runs warn once per backend type without write_blocks X16 Progress keys (time, final_lead_time, member_id) in per-rank logs; bad lines skipped X17 Items are marked done only after outputs flush, the scorer finishes and sync returns X18 Rank 0 lists remaining items and broadcasts them X19 A manifest mismatch raises ValueError unless the progress store overwrites X20 A run or close failure on any rank raises on every rank at the end of run X21 With sync, every rank calls it once per round, idle ranks with None X22 With source_member, slots read from ensemble sources fetch the item's mapped members

Tests live in test/run/. X7, X9's collectives, X13, X18, X20 and X21 run under torchrun with two CPU ranks on gloo; the rest run single-process.

docs.title: Out of scope
docs.text: Explicit model state, initialize/step, components, ports and schedules belong to the model contract and the coupler. Mid-item checkpointing could become an optional runner capability built on (y, state) (open decision 3).

docs.title: Phasing
docs.text:
1. Done. Runner, WorkItem, DataRequest and the built-in runners.
  2. Pipeline. Done: run/work.py, the runner follow-up, run/output.py and run/pipeline.py. Next: replace the eval forecast, diagnostic and dlesym pipelines with built-in runners.
  3. Coupled runner. CoupledRunner is done (E2S-12_COUPLING_SPEC.md), and dev/examples/11_stormscope_coupling.py runs the Flash StormScope GOES and MRMS models as coupled components (GPU check pending). Next: compare against the eval stormscope pipeline and replace it.
  4. Workflows. run.deterministic, run.diagnostic and run.ensemble become thin wrappers over Pipeline.from_model.

docs.title: Resolved decisions
docs.text:
• torch.distributed directly; physicsnemo optional.
  • Core has only the Scorer and sync hooks; metrics and rank communication stay in recipes.
  • Member grouping lives in work_items, since groups are part of item identity.
  • Perturbations are a runner argument (perturbation=, per component for CoupledRunner), drawn per member under member_seed.
  • Plain mappings for per-stream settings and backends.
  • Only Pipeline runs collectives; output and progress stores are rank-local.
  • Distributed stores need blocks of 1 along time and ensemble, which backends report through an optional write_blocks.

docs.title: Open decisions
docs.text:
1. Dependent work items, such as warm-start cycling: v1 or out of scope?
  2. Ensembles: per-element seeding of stochastic batches; bred vectors (model runs, own source, +/- pairs) and lagged ensembles in the runners.
  3. Mid-item resume: must run.* keep step-level checkpoint resume? If so, runners need an optional checkpoint built on (y, state). Blocks phase 4 only.
  4. Async fetching: if needed, change runner and Pipeline loop together.

docs.title: Integration checks
docs.text:
1. PrognosticRunner matches run.deterministic — test/run/test_runner.py.
  2. A hand-written runner stops early and returns None data requests — dev/examples/06_runner.py.
  3. Pipeline drives PrognosticRunner and DiagnosticRunner identically, writing one store per stream — test/run/test_pipeline.py; CoupledRunner too — test/coupling/test_coupled_pipeline.py.
  4. A forced model (StormCast-shaped mock) and fused DLESyM run through PrognosticRunner unchanged.
  5. The DLESyM components through the coupled runner reproduce the fused model — test_dlesym_coupled_reproduces_fused in test/models/px/test_dlesym.py; examples/06_seasonal/02_dlesym_example.py runs both under Pipeline.
  6. Resume survives a world-size change — torchrun, two CPU ranks, gloo, test/run/test_pipeline.py.
  7. The StormScope coupled runner matches the eval stormscope pipeline.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Run several models together, each at its own cadence and on its own grid, with fields passed between them, and run the result under Pipeline like any other Runner. Components are ordinary models: the coupler never wraps, subclasses or mutates them, so every component also runs alone and under its conformance checker.

Status: earth2studio.coupling exports Connector, CoupledRunner and CouplingError. Tests are in test/coupling/; the tutorials are dev/examples/10_coupling.py and dev/examples/11_stormscope_coupling.py. DLESyMAtmos and DLESyMOcean are the atmosphere and ocean of the fused DLESyM as standalone models; examples/06_seasonal/02_dlesym_example.py couples them.

Lineage: this replaces the nvcoupler prototype of PR #1229, which grew out of PR #1114 (the hand-computable toy models, lagged versus sequential coupling and the DLESyM split originate there), and keeps their intent (connectors between components, a derived schedule, eager validation and a readable plan) while building on the model, regrid, time-statistics and execution contracts. The impact-modeling requirements it serves are in the earth2-impact-modeling docs (CR1–CR7).

docs.title: Interface
docs.text:
from earth2studio.coupling import Connector, CoupledRunner

runner = CoupledRunner(
    {"weather": weather_model, "soil": soil_model},
    [Connector("weather", "soil", regridder=to_soil)],
    sources={"weather": weather_ic, "soil": (soil_ic, None, retrievals)},
)
print(runner.describe(np.timedelta64(72, "h")))
Pipeline(runner, output={"weather": w, "soil": s}).run(items)

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Connector:
    src: str
    dst: str
    slot: int = 0
    variables: Mapping[str, str] | Sequence[str] | None = None  # fed base -> src variable; None feeds all
    regridder: Regridder | None = None
    time: Literal["exact", "hold"] = "exact"
    state: bool = False

class CoupledRunner:  # satisfies earth2studio.run.Runner
    supports_member_batching = True
    def __init__(
        self, components, connectors=(), sources=None, seed=0, devices=None,
        source_member=None, perturbation=None,
    ): ...
    def describe(self, final_lead_time) -> str: ...
    def to(self, device) -> CoupledRunner: ...
    def device_of(self, name) -> torch.device: ...
    def output_coords(self, final_lead_time) -> Mapping[str, CoordinateSystem]: ...
    def data_requests(self, item) -> tuple[DataRequest, ...]: ...
    def run_item(self, item) -> Iterator[Mapping[str, xr.DataArray]]: ...

sources maps a component to one source per input-then-forcing slot, in the order of default_sources(); a single source covers the first input slot and None entries fall back to the model's recommendation, which is built only when a fetch needs it. CouplingError is a ValueError. A sequence of variables keeps each name.

devices pins components that to leaves in place, such as CPU-only impact models; the rest move with to. Each component's fetches and connected fields are staged onto its device, and a connector's regridder runs there.

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
Protocol Runs Calls PrognosticModel Every cadence initialize(*x, *forcing), then step(*y, *forcing, state=state) StatefulAssimilationModel Every cadence As above; DataFrame slots may be None DiagnosticModel At each valid time its inputs arrive model(*inputs)

A component may have several gridded output slots. A stateful component's output slots share their lead times; models whose outputs advance at different cadences, such as fused DLESyM, are split into components. The cadence is the model's step interval: the outputs' last lead time minus the later of the first input slot's last lead time and zero. Output chunk k covers the output lead times plus k cadences and is due at its last lead time; chunk 0 comes from initialize. A component whose forcing reduces a day of another's output therefore initializes once that day exists, with no special case.

Imports are a stateful component's time-varying gridded forcing slots, or a diagnostic's input slots. Connectors feed an import: each feeds the labels its variables names, or every label without variables, so several connectors can feed one slot from different producers. Labels no connector feeds, and every other slot, are fetched from sources. Input slots, static forcing and DataFrame slots are always fetched. A diagnostic input slot without lead_time, as most diagnostics declare, takes the call's valid time as a leading dimension, as under DiagnosticRunner.

A state slot is a stateful component's input slot whose output slot in the same position declares its variables on its grid. A state connector (state=True) overwrites the variables it names there before each call, for models that carry a coupled field such as SST in their own state: in the inputs initialize receives, at the input slot's lead times, and in the output each step advances, at its lead times. Several state connectors may share a slot if they overwrite different variables. Required times resolve as for imports, except that values the producer cannot supply at or before the item time are kept rather than fetched. The overwrite is not published; streams carry each model's own output.

docs.title: Connectors and resolution
docs.text:
For each call, every import needs a set of valid times, following the model contract: initialize takes the whole forcing window; step takes the window's final lead time shifted by each lead time of the output it advances; a diagnostic takes the valid time it is called for. For each required time T and slot label:

  1. Split the label: tp:sum:24h is base tp with modifier sum:24h. Map the base through variables to the producer's variable, which exactly one of the producer's output slots publishes.
  2. Plain label, exact: the producer's frame at T. Plain label, hold: the latest frame at or before T that the producer published on an earlier tick. Qualified label: the producer's frames in (T - w, T] at its frame spacing, reduced with apply_time_statistic.
  3. If the producer cannot supply it and T is at or before the item time, a stateful consumer fetches it from the slot's source. A window ending after the item time whose only missing frames are at or before it, as when the producer publishes no initial condition, takes those frames of the base variable from the slot's source and reduces them with the producer's. Otherwise the consumer waits: frames after the item time always come from the producer.
  4. Stage producer frames onto the consumer's device, regrid them with the connector's regridder, then map onto the slot signature with the slot's temporal-statistics metadata.

Connectors select, reduce and regrid; they do not convert. Derived variables, unit changes and vertical levels are a DiagnosticModel component placed between the models, such as DerivedWS for wind speed or DerivedPressureLevels, which interpolates pressure or model levels onto pressure levels. The component publishes its own stream, so conversions are visible in describe and in the outputs.

docs.title: Scheduling
docs.text:
Ticks are the lead times at which some stateful component's chunk is due. Before the first tick, every stateful component fetches its inputs, holds them as frames at their lead times, and publishes an initial condition for each output slot that declares its same-position input slot's variables on the same grid. State slots come first under the model contract, so output-only slots start at the first chunk. At each tick, components run in declaration order whenever their imports resolve, repeating until nothing more can run. A component whose import waits on a frame published later runs later; a diagnostic runs once per valid time at which all its exact inputs exist.

Lagged and sequential coupling are not declared. An exact slot needing a frame at the same valid time as its producer's output runs after it; a hold slot, or one declaring an earlier lead time, lags. A loop of exact edges cannot run and is reported as a cycle.

Construction dry-runs the schedule over two periods of the cadences' least common multiple beyond the latest first chunk. The same scheduler drives describe, output_coords, data_requests and run_item, so a plan cannot drift from a run. Frames older than the oldest one any consumer read in that dry run, plus the longest cadence, are dropped as the run advances.

Known limitation: early reduction windows are partly backfilled from sources, so the dry run can see a long window below its full width. A window much longer than its consumer's step (about 30 h or more for a 6 h consumer, 96 h or more for a 24 h consumer) can then need older frames than are kept, and the run fails partway with a CouplingError that names the history kept for the producer. No shipped model or example reads such a window.

A work item's final lead time must be a lead time at which some stateful component's output is due; any other value raises in describe, output_coords, data_requests and run_item, as PrognosticRunner raises for a final lead time that is not a multiple of its step. A slower component still stops at its last whole chunk.

Components' iterator hooks (front_hook, rear_hook) are not run: the runner calls initialize and step, which apply no hooks (MODEL_CONTRACT P10). The runner logs a warning at construction when a stateful component sets one. Use perturbation= for the initial condition, or a diagnostic component or connector for per-step changes.

docs.title: Streams
docs.text: Each output slot yields one stream: named after the component when it has one output slot, else name.0, name.1 and so on. Stream names must be unique. A stateful slot publishes its initial condition, when it has one, and every chunk; a diagnostic slot publishes at every call. Streams carry the producing model's grid and the item's time, as X1–X4 require. Seeding follows X5, from a base seed offset per component by the CRC-32 of its name, so stochastic components draw independent noise. perturbation maps stateful component names to initial-condition perturbations, applied to the first input slot per member as X6 requires, from the same offset seed. With source_member, every fetched slot whose source is an ensemble source reads the item's mapped member, as X22 requires; connected slots read what their producer published, and DataFrame slots are shared. Batched members travel on a leading ensemble dimension through connectors, buffers, time statistics, regridders and state connectors; one observation frame serves every member, so a DA component must accept a batched background with unbatched observations.

docs.title: Independent assimilation models
docs.text:
An AssimilationModel without initialize and step, such as HealDA, computes one analysis per call from observation DataFrames, with no lead times. It is not a component today: as a diagnostic it would have no connected input to tell it when to run, so the runner rejects its DataFrame slots. It fits elsewhere:

  • As a source. Initializing a prognostic model from HealDA means its input slot's source is an analysis. A DataSource adapter fetches each observation slot at the requested times, calls the model and returns the analysis, so it serves PrognosticRunner and CoupledRunner alike, behind RegriddedSource when grids differ. Models still never fetch (P22); the adapter does.
  • As a component, later. Publishing analyses on a schedule during a run needs components that run on a fixed cadence from sources alone.
  • Cycling is different. An analysis that replaces a prognostic model's state mid-run, with a forecast as background, is a StatefulAssimilationModel, or warm-start work items (execution contract open decision 1).

docs.title: Rules
docs.text: Rule Requirement C1 Components are prognostic, stateful assimilation or diagnostic models with gridded output slots; a stateful component's slots carry the same lead_time C2 Stateful components step at their declared cadence; diagnostics run when their inputs arrive and need at least one exact connector C3 Connectors target a time-varying gridded forcing slot or a diagnostic input slot; several may feed one slot if their labels differ; state connectors target state slots and may share one if their variables differ C4 Every label a connector feeds has a base that, after variables, exactly one producer output slot publishes; variables names declared bases C5 Without a regridder each producer slot read and the consumer slot have the same geometry; with one, its source grid matches each slot read and its target grid the consumer slot C6 Required valid times follow the model contract; DataFrame slots are requested at the chunk's end, static slots only initially C7 exact waits for frames at each required time; hold takes the latest earlier-published frame and applies to plain labels only C8 Qualified labels reduce producer frames over (T - w, T]; the window must divide by the producer's frame spacing C9 Frames at or before the item time that the producer does not hold come from the slot's source, for stateful consumers only, including the early frames of a window ending later; state connectors keep the model's own values instead C10 An empty DataFrame from a source is passed as None C11 A stateful chunk due by the final lead time that cannot run raises, naming the cycle or the missing frame; construction checks this first C12 One uniquely named stream per output slot; describe, output_coords and data_requests come from the scheduler that runs the item; data_requests lists fetch_data calls only, not DataFrame fetches

docs.title: Out of scope or future work
docs.text:
• Time interpolation and conservative regridding. Unit conversion and vertical interpolation are diagnostic components, such as DerivedPressureLevels.
  • A DataSource adapter over independent assimilation models, with per-member seeding when they are stochastic.
  • Components that run on a fixed cadence from sources alone, such as observation-only analyses.
  • DataFrame payloads through connectors, and DataFrame-valued streams.
  • Output slots that advance at different lead times; split them, as for DLESyM.
  • Mid-item checkpoints and iterator hooks on coupled models.
  • Fields with a level dimension. Levels are encoded in variable names; a diagnostic component can map other layouts onto them.
  • Training rollouts: nothing differentiates through the exchange, which stages and regrids frames outside autograd.

docs.title: Open decisions
docs.text:
1. Units. Connected slots exchange lexicon units. A lexicon units table would let connectors reject renames across units and sums over rates.
  2. DataFrame streams. Runner.run_item yields DataArrays only, which blocks tabular products such as TC tracks as coupled outputs.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Provide one shared layer for reading rasters indexed by SpatioTemporal Asset Catalogs (STAC): catalog search, asset href signing and lazy, windowed reads of cloud-optimized GeoTIFFs. Collection-specific data sources (Landsat Collection 2, Sentinel-2 L2A, NAIP, ...) build on it instead of each carrying its own COG reader, and users can call it directly to explore a catalog before a source exists.

The layer is not a DataSource. It returns fields in the asset's native projected grid; packing onto a fixed grid, vocabulary mapping and the DataSource contract belong to the sources built on top (see Collection sources).

Status: implemented in earth2studio/data/stac.py with providers for Microsoft Planetary Computer and Element 84 Earth Search. No collection source exists yet.

docs.title: Interface
docs.text:
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class StacProvider:
    name: str
    api_url: str
    sign: Callable[[str, Mapping[str, Any]], str] = _sign_generic

PLANETARY_COMPUTER: StacProvider
EARTH_SEARCH: StacProvider

def search_items(collection: str, *, provider=PLANETARY_COMPUTER, bbox=None,
                 intersects=None, time_range=None, query=None, cql2_filter=None,
                 ids=None, sortby=None, max_items=100) -> list[pystac.Item]
def open_asset(item: pystac.Item, asset: str, *, provider=None, chunks=1024,
               rescale=True, mask_nodata=True) -> xr.DataArray
def search(collection: str, assets=None, *, provider=PLANETARY_COMPUTER, bbox=None,
           intersects=None, time_range=None, query=None, cql2_filter=None,
           ids=None, sortby=None, max_items=10, chunks=1024, rescale=True,
           mask_nodata=True, lazy=True) -> xr.DataArray
def collections(provider=PLANETARY_COMPUTER, *, bbox=None, text=None,
                sample_assets=True) -> list[dict[str, Any]]
  • search_items runs the STAC query and returns the matching items.
  • open_asset opens one asset of one item as a dask-backed array in its native grid.
  • search composes the two: it opens the requested assets of every matching item, clips them to bbox and stacks them into (time, variable, y, x).
  • collections lists a catalog's collections with asset keys and overall extents.
  • StacProvider.sign turns an asset href plus the merged item/asset properties (and the item's collection id) into a path GDAL can read. Signing is the only provider-specific code; everything else is catalog agnostic.

Each argument takes one form: collection is one id, assets a sequence of asset keys, time_range an ISO 8601 interval string, provider a StacProvider. The STAC filter extension is exposed as cql2_filter (CQL2-JSON) and ids; arbitrary keyword passthrough to the client is not supported.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
Rule Requirement S1 Opening reads the file header only; pixels are read on compute, tile by tile S2 Arrays keep the asset's native CRS and affine transform S3 raster:bands nodata, scale and offset are applied per band S4 Masked nodata is NaN; unmasked data keeps the file dtype S5 A nodata not shared by all stacked bands or variables is dropped, not misreported S6 Signing never writes to the process environment S7 Planetary Computer tokens are fetched and renewed by GDAL, one per collection S8 search returns (time, variable, y, x) sorted by time on the first asset's grid S9 Layers on another grid are resampled onto it from a padded clip S10 Item time is datetime, else start_datetime, as UTC datetime64 S11 Items that miss bbox are skipped; a sub-pixel bbox raises ValueError S12 Multi-band assets become one variable per band, labelled <asset>_<band> S13 earth2studio.data imports rasterio before any ECMWF library
  • S1: only the COG tiles a computation touches are fetched. search has one exception, S9: resampling is eager for the clipped window of the layers that need it.
  • S2: da.rio.crs and da.rio.transform() hold the geometry, carried by spatial_ref and the y, x dimension coordinates. This is what ProjectedGrid(y, x, crs) describes (E2S-02_GRID_SPEC.md); earth2studio_crs is not written by this layer.
  • S3: a band without an entry falls back to the file's nodata and scale/offset tags; once applied, the scale tags are removed from attrs so CF decoders do not apply them again.
  • S4: with mask_nodata=False the declared nodata is rescaled alongside the values. Integer inputs promote to float32 (8/16-bit) or float64 (wider) only when masking or scaling applies.
  • S6: GDAL options travel in the path (/vsicurl?opt=val&url=...); credentials and process-wide tuning are read from the environment the user set. Requester-pays buckets return /vsis3/ paths and need AWS_REQUEST_PAYER=requester plus AWS credentials; a warning is logged when the variable is unset.
  • S7: GDAL's pc_url_signing with pc_collection; the module keeps no token cache, so lazy arrays stay readable past a token's lifetime.
  • S8: attrs["stac_items"] lists the item ids in time order; per-asset attrs (stac_item, stac_asset, href) are not carried over. List the finest-resolution asset first to keep full resolution.
  • S9: nearest neighbour from a clip padded by two pixels, so pixels straddling the window edge survive. Uncovered pixels are the declared nodata, or NaN (promoting to float) when none is declared.
  • S10: a naive datetime is UTC. Items with neither field get NaT and sort last.
  • S11: "miss" means no pixel of an asset intersects bbox; "sub-pixel" means the box covers fewer than two pixels of an asset.
  • S13: loading eccodes first makes every GDAL /vsicurl read segfault on Linux.

docs.title: Collection sources
docs.text:
A source for a particular collection is a thin class over this layer that owns what the layer deliberately does not:

  • Grid: declare a ProjectedGrid (or lat/lon LatLonGrid) and resample or mosaic the per-scene windows from search onto it, one field per requested time. Where several scene footprints cover the request, the source decides how to combine them; this layer returns one window per scene.
  • Request: translate a Region (E2S-02_GRID_SPEC.md) into bbox, and the DataSource time array into a time_range plus item selection (nearest scene, cloud-cover sort, time tolerance).
  • Vocabulary: map E2STUDIO_VOCAB ids to asset keys (and bands of multi-band assets) through a lexicon.
  • Contract: meet DataSource (E2S-05_FETCH_DATA_SPEC.md), including the device convention: compute the dask array and return NumPy on CPU or CuPy on CUDA. RegriddedSource (E2S-04_REGRID_SPEC.md) then maps the source onto a model grid without further code here.
  • Coupling: a collection source is bound to a model slot through Coupler(sources=...) (E2S-12_COUPLING_SPEC.md); the coupler stages it onto the model device and regrids it like any source, so the layer needs nothing coupler-specific.

docs.title: Deferred Work and Verification
docs.text:
• First collection source (candidate: Landsat Collection 2 Level-2) and its mosaic rule; nothing in this layer prejudges whether the fixed grid is projected or lat/lon.
  • Resampling methods other than nearest neighbour for S9.
  • Verification: test/data/test_stac.py covers signing, calibration, per-band metadata, grid alignment (incl. S9 edge pixels and fill), time handling and catalog listing offline (local GeoTIFFs, a local HTTP server for the /vsicurl path form, a fake STAC client); two slow tests read the live catalogs.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Base Install Limitations

Base install scope: The base install includes only core Earth2Studio APIs. Most models, data sources, examples, and workflows require an optional dependency group selected below.

GPU dependency compatibility: GPU-dependent model dependencies can be sensitive to the PyTorch and CUDA versions in your environment.

Prerequisites

  • PyTorch: See the PyTorch install guide and make sure PyTorch is installed correctly on your system first.
  • Python environment: Initialize an appropriate Python environment. Python 3.13 is the recommended version.
  • Package manager: uv is recommended, but pip is also supported.

docs.title: GPU Dependency Wheels
docs.text:
FlashAttention and NATTEN can take a long time to build. Before building from source, check for prebuilt wheels compatible with the model's requirements, Python ABI, OS/architecture, PyTorch build, CUDA build, and GPU capability. Use torch.__version__ and torch.version.cuda to identify the Torch build; the CUDA version shown by nvidia-smi alone is not sufficient.

  • FlashAttention: check the Astral GPU indexes and uv's extension guide. Select a matching wheel, use a named [[tool.uv.index]] with explicit = true, and map flash-attn to that index in [tool.uv.sources].
  • NATTEN: check the installation guide, including older builds, and prebuilt wheels. Pin the compatible build including its +torch...cu... suffix when applicable and use --find-links https://whl.natten.org with uv add or pip install. Persist find-links in [tool.uv] for uv projects. Models requiring libnatten need that backend, not just an importable NATTEN package; check natten.HAS_LIBNATTEN when supported by the installed version.

Configure these sources in your own project; Earth2Studio's uv settings are not inherited when installed as a dependency. Preserve existing Torch pins unless you choose a compatible environment change. If no matching wheel exists, follow the dependency's source-build requirements. Custom/NGC Torch builds may require compilation rather than an official-release wheel.

docs.title: Verify Installation
docs.text:
python -c "import earth2studio; print(earth2studio.__version__)"

If you installed with uv and want to run inside the uv project:

uv run python -c "import earth2studio; print(earth2studio.__version__)"

docs.title: Environments
docs.text: For the best experience, create a fresh environment with uv, Docker, or another environment manager. For developer environments, refer to the Developer Overview.

docs.title: uv Project
docs.text:
Using uv is the recommended way to set up a local Python environment for Earth2Studio. Assuming uv is installed, use the following commands:

mkdir earth2studio-project && cd earth2studio-project
uv init --python=3.13
uv add "earth2studio @ git+https://github.com/NVIDIA/earth2studio.git@0.20.0"

docs.title: Docker Container
docs.text:
For a Docker environment, the recommended process is to use uv inside a container. The NVIDIA PyTorch container typically provides a good base with many dependencies already installed and optimized for NVIDIA hardware.

docker run -it -t nvcr.io/nvidia/pytorch:26.04-py3

apt-get update && apt-get install -y git make curl cmake python3-dev \
    libeccodes-tools libeccodes-dev
unset PIP_CONSTRAINT
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh && source $HOME/.local/bin/env
uv pip install --system --break-system-packages \
    "earth2studio @ git+https://github.com/NVIDIA/earth2studio.git@0.20.0"

Extra Dependencies

Add extras to the uv pip install command in the same way you would for pip:

uv pip install --system --break-system-packages \
    "earth2studio[aifs,data] @ git+https://github.com/NVIDIA/earth2studio.git@0.20.0"
Earth2Studio in Docker

Some models and dependencies have specific system requirements, such as CUDA versions, that may require a different container. If you are comfortable with Docker, refer to the testing Dockerfile as a reference for a general-purpose Earth2Studio image.

docs.title: Conda Environment
docs.text:
It is no longer recommended to use conda environment managers for Earth2Studio when uv is available. If conda is required for your system, use it only to create the Python environment and install Earth2Studio with standard Python tooling.

conda create -n earth2studio python=3.13
conda activate earth2studio
pip install earth2studio

docs.title: Software
docs.text:
Earth2Studio does not have specific software version requirements. The following versions are recommended to closely match development and automation environments:

  • OS: Ubuntu 24.04 LTS
  • Python Version: 3.13
  • CUDA Version: 13.0

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text:
Earth2Studio does not have specific hardware requirements. If PyTorch can run, many features of Earth2Studio should run as well. Most models do require a GPU with sufficient memory and compute capability.

GPU GPU Memory (GB) Precision # of GPUs Disk Space (GB) NVIDIA GPU with compute capability >= 8.9 >=40 FP32 1 128

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Earth2Studio uses a few environment variables to configure package behavior:

  • EARTH2STUDIO_CACHE: General cache location for models and cached data. Defaults to ~/.cache/earth2studio.
  • EARTH2STUDIO_DATA_CACHE: Cache location for data sources. If set, this overrides EARTH2STUDIO_CACHE for data source caching.
  • EARTH2STUDIO_MODEL_CACHE: Cache location for model packages. If set, this overrides EARTH2STUDIO_CACHE for model checkpoint caching.
  • EARTH2STUDIO_PACKAGE_TIMEOUT: Maximum number of seconds for a model package download from a remote store such as NGC, Hugging Face, or S3.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: This page has moved to the User Guide overview.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Earth2Studio provides composable building blocks for AI weather and climate inference. Chain models so raw observations can flow through analyses, forecasts, and application-specific products to support a decision.

Bring your own model at any stage. Start with an existing analysis or forecast, use an individual component, or assemble a workflow entirely from built-in blocks. Community and proprietary models can share one pipeline through the same interfaces.

docs.title: Building Blocks
docs.text:
Each component has a focused role. Choose the pieces your application needs:

Component Role in a workflow Data and metadata Describe what data means. Data sources Fetch fields, forecasts, or observations. Data assimilation Ingest, predict and assimilate sparse observations. Prognostic models Advance a forecast through time. Diagnostic models Derive variables, downscale, or transform fields. Perturbations Create alternative initial conditions. Statistics Summarize ensembles and evaluate predictions. IO backends Stream labelled data products to memory or storage.

Regridding aligns spatial domains between components. Execution tools coordinate the work, while checkpointing lets supported workflows resume. You can replace a block with a local implementation without replacing the rest of the pipeline.

docs.title: A Basic Forecast Pipeline
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Data source] --> B[Forecast loop]
    B --> C[Output stream]
  1. Fetch initial conditions. A data source supplies the fields needed by the model, prepared for its variables, history, grid, and device.
  2. Advance the forecast. The forecast loop initializes a trajectory and steps the model forward, producing labelled forecast chunks.
  3. Stream the results. An IO backend writes each output as it becomes available. Downstream components can also transform or score those fields.

docs.title: From Observations to Decisions
docs.text:
This basic pipeline can grow increasingly complex as you connect more components. The goal is to enable AI-driven forecasting pipelines that support real-world decision-making. A more complete pipeline might look like this:

flowchart LR
    A[Observations] --> B[Data assimilation model]
    B --> C[Forecast model]
    C --> D[Diagnostic model]
    D --> E[Decision model]

Build bespoke pipelines using Earth2Studio's selection of open models, your own custom models, or a combination of both. Bring your own open or proprietary data through data-source interfaces, including observations, initial conditions, and existing forecasts. Assemble these components around your application to create a workflow with its own unique value.

docs.title: Constructing Pipelines
docs.text:
Use components directly in Python or assemble them with the execution tools:

  • Pipeline (earth2studio.run) manages work items such as initialization times, forecast horizons, and ensemble members. It handles output selection, regridding, storage, optional scoring, distribution, and resuming completed work. Pipeline.from_model(...) builds a prognostic runner from a model and data sources, with optional diagnostics.
  • CoupledRunner (earth2studio.coupling) connects models through Connector declarations. Connectors describe which producer supplies a consumer's inputs, including variable mapping, time selection, and optional regridding. The runner schedules components at their own cadences and fetches externally supplied inputs.

Pass a CoupledRunner to Pipeline to manage a coupled system with the same output and work-management tools as a single-model forecast.

docs.title: Built for People and Agents
docs.text:
Rich metadata makes component inputs and outputs inspectable. An agent can examine variables, grids, times, and schemas to propose connections and check compatibility before execution. Data products retain labels and metadata that downstream agents and applications can use to interpret their results.

Earth2Studio's agentic skills provide workflows for discovering components, preparing data, running inference, and wrapping custom models. These tools help an agent build and validate a pipeline against explicit interfaces; your reference cases establish that a custom model still produces the intended predictions.

docs.title: Where To Go Next
docs.text:
• Install Earth2Studio and the model dependencies you need.
  • Start with Data and Metadata, then explore the core components.
  • Run the examples for complete workflows.
  • Wrap your own model with agent-assisted guidance in your own project.

docs.title: AutoModels
docs.text:
Earth2Studio offers a selection of pre-trained model checkpoints. The fetching and caching of the model's checkpoint files is the responsibility of the earth2studio.models.auto.AutoModelMixin and earth2studio.models.auto.Package classes. Understanding how these classes work can help users customize where model checkpoints are stored as well as how to add their own pre-trained model to the package.

Model weights for Earth2Studio can be stored in a variety of locations that make them publicly accessible to users. When contributing a model, reach out with an issue to discuss the storage of such files. Providing all checkpoint files is a requirement for any pre-trained model. The following are the suggested locations in order of preference:

  • NGC Model Registry - If a model is supported/developed by Nvidia PhysicsNeMo team, the checkpoint can be uploaded on the NGC model registry. This is the preferred location for Nvidia supported models that have gone under a more rigorous internal evaluation. Private registries are also supported.

  • Huggingface Model Registry - Huggingface offers model registries that any user can upload and share checkpoint files with. This is the method used for model files of several models that are not developed or trained by Nvidia.

  • S3 Object Storage - Providing model checkpoints with a S3 bucket is also another viable object assuming the egress cost for downloads are covered by the owner.

docs.title: AutoModelMixin
docs.text:
The earth2studio.models.auto.AutoModelMixin class provides the interface that pre-trained models in Earth2Studio use. Any automodel in Earth2Studio needs to implement both the load_default_package and load_model functions.

Method Purpose load_default_package() Return the default Package pointing at the model assets. load_model(package) Instantiate the model and load weights from the provided package.

load_default_package is typically simple to implement, typically a single line of code that creates the earth2studio.models.auto.Package object. load_model does the heavy lifting, instantiating the model and loading the pre-trained weights. All pre-trained models in Earth2Studio implement these methods. For example, have a look at the FourCastNet implementations:



    @classmethod
    @check_optional_dependencies()
    def load_model(
        cls,
        package: Package,
    ) -> PrognosticModel:
        """Load prognostic from package"""
        try:
            package.resolve("config.json")  # HF tracking download statistics
        except FileNotFoundError:
            pass

        model = AFNO.from_checkpoint(package.resolve("fcn.mdlus"))
        model.eval()

        local_center = torch.Tensor(np.load(package.resolve("global_means.npy")))
        local_std = torch.Tensor(np.load(package.resolve("global_stds.npy")))
        return cls(model, center=local_center, scale=local_std)

Note

The load_default_package doesn't perform any downloading. Rather, it creates a pointer to the directory the checkpoint files exist in, offering a primitive abstract filesystem. load_model triggers the download of any files when the path is accessed using package.get("local/dir/to/file").

docs.title: Package
docs.text:
The earth2studio.models.auto.Package class is an abstract representation of a storage location that contains some artifacts used to load a pre-trained model. This class abstracts away the download and caching of files on the local machine. Given that a supported remote store type is used, the use of the package class is as follows:

from earth2studio.models.auto import Package

# Instantiate package by pointing it to a remote folder
package = Package("ngc://models/nvidia/modulus/modulus_fcn@v0.2")

# Fetch a file from the remote store using the resolve method
cached_path_to_file = package.resolve("fcn.zip")

# Open a buffered reader of the file
opened_file = package.open("fcn.zip")

In this example, when calling resolve or open, the asset at ngc://models/nvidia/modulus/modulus_fcn@v0.2/fcn.zip will be fetched and cached on the local machine. A file buffer will then be returned pointing to the cached version of the file. The cached path is a directory on the local file system, which can be configured using environment variables. See Configuration section for details.

Note

Earth2Studio file system uses Fsspec caching for files in packages. We encourage users that are interested in this type of utility to learn more about Fsspec and the specification it defines for advanced usage.

docs.title: Batch Dimension
docs.text:
This section of the user guide expands on how batching is handled inside Earth2Studio. As discussed in Data and Metadata section, there is a dedicated coordinate axis batch which is commonly used in many of the model implementations. batch represents a dynamic axis that can be of any size, enabling models to better utilize compute resources.

Batch dimensions have the following rules:

  • Must be able to support any nonzero size
  • Must be the leading dimensions of the coordinate system
  • Must be set to np.empty(0) in objects coordinate property

docs.title: Good Coordinate Definitions
docs.text:
batch is the leading dimension with a value of np.empty(0).

coords = OrderedDict(
        {
            "batch": np.empty(0),
            "lead_time": np.array([np.timedelta64(0, "h")]),
            "variable": np.array(VARIABLES),
            "lat": np.linspace(90, -90, 720, endpoint=False),
            "lon": np.linspace(0, 360, 1440, endpoint=False),
        }
    )

Other coordinates can have a value of np.empty(0) to denote an additional dynamic axis but imply a required data type. In this case, this model supports a batch but the time axis must be a Numpy array of type np.datetime64. See Data and Metadata page for expected types.

coords = OrderedDict(
        {
            "batch": np.empty(0),
            "time": np.empty(0),
            "variable": np.array(VARIABLES),
            "lat": np.linspace(90, -90, 720, endpoint=False),
            "lon": np.linspace(0, 360, 1440, endpoint=False),
        }
    )

docs.title: Bad Coordinate Definitions
docs.text:
Batch dimension is not leading.

coords = OrderedDict(
        {
            "variable": np.array(VARIABLES),
            "batch": np.empty(0),
            "lat": np.linspace(90, -90, 720, endpoint=False),
            "lon": np.linspace(0, 360, 1440, endpoint=False),
        }
    )

Batch dimension is not of size 0.

coords = OrderedDict(
        {
            "batch": np.zeros(1),
            "variable": np.array(VARIABLES),
            "lat": np.linspace(90, -90, 720, endpoint=False),
            "lon": np.linspace(0, 360, 1440, endpoint=False),
        }
    )

docs.title: Batch Decorator
docs.text:
While the use of batch dimension is useful for communicating a dimension that can accept variable input sizes, it's not very convenient to manually manipulate data into a form that matches the batch dimension. To make using batch supporting models easier, Earth2Studio offers a utility decorator earth2studio.models.batch.batch_func which automates transforming extra leading dimensions into a batch one. This utility must be used in an object with coordinate properties.

The batch function does the following steps:

  1. Squeeze leading dims into a batch dimension
  2. Update batched input coordinates with a single batch index dimension
  3. Execute the wrapped function and get outputs
  4. Replace output batch coord with the batched input coordinates
  5. Unsqueeze the leading batch coordinate into original input dimensions

Coordinate planners preserve leading dimensions directly; output_coords does not need a batching decorator. For DataArray coordinate systems, use coord_array_like to preserve the input's leading dimensions and auxiliary coordinates while updating the model's output coordinates.

Consider the following dictionary-coordinate example:

from collections import OrderedDict

import numpy as np
import torch

from earth2studio.models.batch import batch_func


class BatchModel:
    def input_coords(self) -> OrderedDict:
        return OrderedDict({"batch": np.zeros(0), "dim1": np.arange(2)})

    def output_coords(
        self,
        input_coords: OrderedDict
        ) -> OrderedDict:
        output_coords = input_coords.copy()
        del output_coords["dim1"]
        output_coords["dim2"] = np.arange(4)
        return output_coords

    @batch_func()
    def __call__(self, input, coords):
        print("Model Input:", input.size(), coords)
        out = torch.cat([input, input], dim=-1)
        out_c = self.output_coords(coords).copy()
        return out, out_c


input_coords = OrderedDict(
    {"batched_dim0": np.arange(2), "batched_dim1": np.arange(3), "dim1": np.arange(2)}
)
input = torch.randn(2, 3, 2)

model = BatchModel()
print("Input:", input.size(), input_coords)
output, output_coords = model(input, input_coords)
print("Output:", output.size(), output_coords)

The output of the following script will be:

Input: torch.Size([2, 3, 2]) OrderedDict([('batched_dim0', array([0, 1])), ('bacthed_dim1', array([0, 1, 2])), ('dim1', array([0, 1]))])

Model Input: torch.Size([6, 2]) OrderedDict([('batch', array([0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5])), ('dim1', array([0, 1]))])

Output: torch.Size([2, 3, 4]) OrderedDict([('batched_dim0', array([0, 1])), ('bacthed_dim1', array([0, 1, 2])), ('dim2', array([0, 1, 2, 3]))])

Note that the leading two dimensions were squeezed into a single batch dimension before the execution of the models BatchModel.__call__. The leading dimensions were then restored back while preserving the updated domain coordinates from the model's output.

The batch decorator will also unsqueeze a batch axis to an input that is missing only batch from the input coordinate system with no additional dimensions. In this instance a batch size of one is implied. For example, using the model in the example above:

input_coords = OrderedDict(
    {"dim1": np.arange(2)}
)
input = torch.randn(2)

model = BatchModel()
print("Input:", input.size(), input_coords)
output, output_coords = model(input, input_coords)
print("Output:", output.size(), output_coords)

will execute successfully with an output of:

Input: torch.Size([2]) OrderedDict([('dim1', array([0, 1]))])

Model Input: torch.Size([1, 2]) OrderedDict([('batch', array([0])), ('dim1', array([0, 1]))])

Output: torch.Size([4]) OrderedDict([('dim2', array([0, 1, 2, 3]))])

docs.title: Batch Dimension in IO
docs.text:
The IO backends require users to pre-define the output coordinate system on which the data will be exported. Typically, a good way to do this is to review the output coordinates of the model, which will typically include a dynamic batch dimension. But the model won't actually return a batch dimension, thus it's a common pattern to replace this batch dimension with whatever leading coordinate the input will have.

earth2studio.io.utils.output_template does this, as the built-in workflows do. It replaces the dynamic leading dimensions of the model's output signature with known leading dimensions like time, and replaces fixed labels such as lead_time with the full forecast horizon:

from earth2studio.io.utils import output_template

# (batch, lead_time, variable, lat, lon)
signature = prognostic.output_coords(prognostic.input_coords())
step = signature.coords["lead_time"].values[-1]
template = output_template(
    signature,
    leading={"time": time},  # replaces batch
    coords={"lead_time": np.arange(nsteps + 1) * step},
)
io.add_array(template)  # one (time, lead_time, lat, lon) array per variable

docs.title: Checkpointing
docs.text:
Earth2Studio checkpoints enable users to restart inference workflows. A checkpoint is a catalog of restart points for one named run. Each row in that catalog is a checkpoint session: it records the completed lead time, optional metadata, and opt-in component state(s) needed to restart the workflow.

Checkpoint storage is independent of the user-facing IO backend and independent of any particular model implementation. Forecast fields remain in the IO backend you choose, model weights are not copied into checkpoints, and the checkpoint catalog stores only the restart metadata and component state requested by the configured checkpoint level. Exactly what gets logged is user-configurable through the checkpoint options and through the checkpoint support implemented by each component.

Warning

Checkpointing support is opt-in for every component. Not all models, perturbations, or custom components support checkpointed restarts. Always verify that the model you plan to use has checkpoint support before relying on it for restartable inference. If checkpointing is missing for a model you need, open a feature request.

docs.title: Basic Use
docs.text:
from earth2studio.run import deterministic
from earth2studio.utils.checkpoint import Checkpoint

checkpoint = Checkpoint("my-forecast", flush_interval=6, level=2)

with checkpoint as ckpt:
    deterministic(
        time=["2024-01-01"],
        nsteps=24,
        prognostic=model,
        data=data,
        io=io,
        checkpoint=ckpt,
    )

Use checkpointed workflows inside a checkpoint context. This makes the active session clear and lets restart-aware models or perturbations bind their state before the run starts. Built-in workflows automatically interact with the checkpoint session: they call write after successful IO writes and call flush before returning. If no checkpoint is supplied, they use the NullCheckpoint no-op checkpoint.

Checkpoint options:

  • flush_interval=1: commit every workflow write.
  • flush_interval=None: keep writes pending until flush().
  • mode="overwrite": keep only the latest row.
  • mode="append": keep a row history; cap it with history_size.
  • device=torch.device("cpu"): device used by components for staged tensor state.

Components can opt into checkpoint state when they need restart information (RNG state, counters, tensors, etc.). The user chooses the requested level, and each component decides what it supports:

  • 0: no component logging; workflows still record catalog progress and explicit metadata.
  • 1: enough component state to restart a workflow item such as an ensemble member.
  • 2: full component state for restarting inside a rollout when the component supports it.

docs.title: Selecting Rows
docs.text:
Print a checkpoint to inspect its catalog, then select a row by integer index. Negative indexing is supported.

checkpoint = Checkpoint("my-forecast")

print(checkpoint)

latest = checkpoint.select(-1)
first = checkpoint.select(0)

By default, the context manager with checkpoint selects the latest catalog row when one exists, or opens a new session when the catalog is empty. Use with checkpoint.select(-1): when a specific saved row should be restored.

docs.title: Custom Loops
docs.text:
Call write after a safe restart boundary, usually after forecast fields have been written to IO. Call flush() to force the latest pending write to disk.

checkpoint = Checkpoint("forecast", mode="append", history_size=8)

with checkpoint as ckpt:
    for lead_time in lead_times:
        x = step_model(...)
        io.write(x)
        ckpt.write(
            lead_time=lead_time,
            last_complete_lead_time=lead_time,
        )

    ckpt.flush()

write and flush accept generic keyword metadata. Use metadata for small restart properties; large forecast arrays should remain in the IO backend.

docs.title: Workflow Resume
docs.text:
Built-in workflows, like run.deterministic, always fetch the normal initial condition and pass it to the prognostic iterator. The checkpoint session tells the workflow what has been already completed. For ensemble runs, the workflow records completed_ensembles metadata and resumes from the first incomplete member. Checkpoint-aware models decide whether to restore their own state and, if restored, should yield the next forecast state rather than the existing saved boundary.

This decouples user-facing IO from what might be required to resume a run via a checkpoint: users often save only a subset of generated forecast variables, but continuing a rollout may require all fields and possibly internal model state.

docs.title: Component State
docs.text:
Models, perturbations, and custom components opt in by binding a dataclass. Existing components do not need to change.

from dataclasses import dataclass

import torch

from earth2studio.utils.checkpoint import bind_checkpoint_state


@dataclass
class NoiseState:
    rng_state: torch.Tensor | None = None


class NoisePerturbation:
    def __init__(self, generator: torch.Generator):
        self.generator = generator
        self.checkpoint = bind_checkpoint_state(NoiseState())

        if self.checkpoint.rng_state is not None:
            self.generator.set_state(self.checkpoint.rng_state)

    def __call__(self, x):
        y = add_noise(x, generator=self.generator)
        if self.checkpoint.checkpoint_level >= 1:
            self.checkpoint.rng_state = self.generator.get_state()
        return y

bind_checkpoint_state returns a proxy around the dataclass. Normal dataclass fields are accessed directly. Checkpoint metadata is available through read-only properties such as checkpoint_enabled, checkpoint_level, checkpoint_state_loaded, checkpoint_metadata, checkpoint_lead_time, and device. Use device for staging tensor state, for example x.detach().clone().to(self.checkpoint.device).

Construct restart-aware components inside the checkpoint context when saved state must be restored during initialization:

checkpoint = Checkpoint("my-forecast")

with checkpoint.select(-1) as ckpt:
    model = MyRestartableModel(...)
    deterministic(..., checkpoint=ckpt)

If a component binds before an existing session is active, Earth2Studio restores it when the session opens and warns because constructor side effects may already have used default state.

State identity is the dataclass type's fully qualified module and class name. Binding the same dataclass type twice in one session raises CheckpointStateCollision; use distinct dataclass types for distinct components.

docs.title: Serialization
docs.text:
Checkpoint state is pickle-free. Supported values include JSON-like scalars and containers, dataclasses, datetime, date, timedelta, numpy.datetime64, numpy.timedelta64, NumPy scalars and dtypes, torch.device, torch.dtype, torch.Tensor, and non-object numpy.ndarray. Tensors and arrays are stored as separate .npy files with pickle disabled.

Unsupported values raise CheckpointSerializationError. Incompatible dataclass schema changes raise CheckpointStateSchemaError during restore.

docs.title: Storage
docs.text:
Default location:

$EARTH2STUDIO_CACHE/checkpoints/<name>

or, if EARTH2STUDIO_CACHE is unset:

~/.cache/earth2studio/checkpoints/<name>

Pass path= to choose another location. Serial runs write directly into that folder. Distributed runs write per-rank folders such as rank_000000; rank detection checks PhysicsNeMo's distributed manager first, then common distributed environment variables.

Checkpoint writes are staged in temporary directories and atomically moved into place when complete. Catalog JSON writes use the same temporary-file pattern. Incomplete temporary writes are ignored and cleaned up by later writes.

docs.title: Adaptive Model Domains
docs.text: Some models can run on a selected geographic region rather than only their default domain. Models implementing DomainAdaptable provide with_region(region), which returns a new model view sharing the loaded weights and statics. The original model and other views retain their own domains.

docs.title: Select a Region
docs.text:
The Region object describes a geographic request independently of any model grid. Choose a shape supported by your model:

Constructor Geographic request Region.box(west, south, east, north) Longitude/latitude bounds in degrees. Region.band(south, north) Latitude band spanning all longitudes. Region.circle(lat, lon, radius_m) Center and geodesic radius in metres. Region.rectangle(lat, lon, half_width_m, half_height_m, bearing_deg) Oriented rectangle.

Rectangle sizes are half extents in metres; omitting half_height_m makes a square. The bearing is clockwise from north to the rectangle's positive y axis. A box with west > east crosses the antimeridian; use a band for full-longitude coverage.

Given a loaded model that supports box requests:

from earth2studio.grids import Region, infer_grid
from earth2studio.models.base import DomainAdaptable

if not isinstance(model, DomainAdaptable):
    raise TypeError("This model does not support regional views")

region = Region.box(west=-105.0, south=35.0, east=-100.0, north=40.0)
regional_model = model.with_region(region)

# For a single-input model, inspect the selected input domain.
input_signature = regional_model.input_coords()
input_grid = infer_grid(input_signature)
output_signature = regional_model.output_coords(input_signature)

docs.title: Use the Selected Domain
docs.text:
The region is a request, not the final grid. The model selects compatible input, forcing, and output grids, which may include padding or a larger footprint. Inspect the returned view's coordinate signatures for the actual domain, and prepare inputs against those signatures. For example, pass input_grid as target_grid to fetch_data; multi-input models require preparing each slot separately.

Unsupported shapes or regions that cannot be covered raise ValueError. Coverage describes geometry, not forecast skill outside a model's training region. Select the region before initializing a rollout; start a new trajectory when changing domains rather than reusing incompatible domain-dependent state. Views can run sequentially; concurrent execution depends on the wrapper's documented support.

See Data and Metadata for grid objects and the model domain contract for the full interface requirements.

docs.title: Advanced Output Handling
docs.text: This guide outlines advanced features supported by Earth2Studio IO backends. Start with Output Handling for the common interface and creating output templates. Backend options are listed in the IO API.

docs.title: Versioned Output with Icechunk
docs.text:
IceChunkBackend writes to an Icechunk repository instead of a plain Zarr store. Commits create immutable snapshots, giving an inference campaign a versioned history that can be reopened later.

The backend extends ZarrBackend with commit(message). Its usual template, writing, and reading methods remain available. Install the optional dependency with pip install 'earth2studio[data]'.

Given a prepared output template and an iterable of forecast DataArrays:

from earth2studio.io import IceChunkBackend

io = IceChunkBackend("forecast_repo", branch="main")
io.add_array(template)
for forecast in forecasts:
    io.write(forecast)

snapshot_id = io.commit("forecast run 2024-01-01T00Z")
io.close()

The storage argument accepts a filesystem path or an icechunk.Storage instance; omitting it creates an in-memory repository. A new named branch is created from the tip of main when needed.

Writes are non-blocking by default. read, __getitem__, commit, and close flush pending writes first; use blocking=True for synchronous writes. flush() makes pending writes visible within the open session, while commit() publishes a snapshot and opens a new writable session. close() commits remaining changes with a generic message and rejects later writes. Commit explicitly when you need a descriptive message or conflict handling. Earth2Studio workflows leave closing the backend to the caller.

Reopen a snapshot with repo.readonly_session(snapshot_id=snapshot_id), or create branches with repo.create_branch(...). Icechunk also supports object storage through constructors such as icechunk.s3_storage(...).

Note

An empty commit raises an IcechunkError unless allow_empty=True is supplied. Another writer committing to the same branch can cause a conflict; consult Icechunk's documentation for rebasing and rebase_with. Local filesystem storage is not safe for concurrent commits; use object storage for that case.

docs.title: Asynchronous and Sharded Zarr Output
docs.text:
AsyncZarrBackend overlaps storage writes with inference. Coordinates listed in parallel_coords have chunk size one, allowing separate forecast slices to be written independently. Large campaigns can consequently produce many small files. Zarr v3 sharding groups chunks into fewer storage objects:

from collections import OrderedDict

from earth2studio.io import AsyncZarrBackend

io = AsyncZarrBackend(
    "forecast.zarr",
    parallel_coords=OrderedDict({"time": times, "lead_time": lead_times}),
    shard_coords={"lead_time": 8},
)
io.add_array(template)
for forecast in forecasts:
    io.write(forecast)
io.close()

Here times and lead_times contain the full output coordinate labels. Eight lead-time chunks share one shard; readers can still select individual chunks. Writes must cover the non-parallel dimensions in full. Define the layout before writing, and close the backend to finish pending work.

docs.title: Choosing a Shard Size
docs.text:
The backend buffers chunks in host memory and writes a complete shard together, avoiding repeated read-modify-write operations. Balance three costs:

  • Host memory: budget approximately max_inflight_shards * 4 * shard_bytes + pool_size * write_bytes per process. Encoded copies and concurrent flushes add to the shard buffer itself. A 73-variable, 721-by-1440 float32 field is about 0.3 GB per lead; eight leads require about 2.4 GB for one buffer before those extra costs.
  • Storage bandwidth: max_inflight_shards controls concurrent shard flushes. Raising it helps only until bandwidth saturates. Distributed ranks already add concurrency, so fewer in-flight shards per rank may be appropriate.
  • Production rate: asynchronous writing hides IO latency when storage keeps pace with inference. If it cannot, reduce output volume or use faster storage.

Measure the tradeoff between memory, throughput, and file count on your storage system. Compression through zarr_codecs applies to the inner chunks. chunked_coords sets chunk sizes for non-parallel dimensions; parallel dimensions remain chunked at one. Each shard size must be a multiple of its chunk size.

docs.title: Partial Shards and Restarts
docs.text: close() flushes incomplete shards, leaving unsupplied positions at the array fill value. Writing into an existing shard falls back to read-modify-write and logs a warning. This can happen after a mid-run flush() or when resuming a partial run. Align restart boundaries with shard boundaries to retain the complete-shard fast path.

docs.title: Multiple Processes Writing One Store
docs.text:
Warning

Each shard must belong to exactly one process. Buffers are process-local: two ranks writing different chunks in the same shard can each overwrite the whole shard, silently discarding the other's data. Read-modify-write does not protect against concurrent writers.

Shard along an axis each rank owns completely. For example, when ranks own distinct initialization times and all leads for each forecast, sharding lead_time is safe:

io = AsyncZarrBackend(
    "forecast.zarr",
    parallel_coords=OrderedDict({"time": all_times, "lead_time": all_lead_times}),
    shard_coords={"lead_time": 8},
)

Sharding the distributed time axis is safe only if every rank's assigned indexes form whole shards. For example, splitting eight times across three ranks into blocks 0–2, 3–5, and 6–7 crosses a shard boundary when shard_coords={"time": 4}. That layout lets two ranks overwrite the same shard. Ownership must remain valid when the number of ranks or work items changes.

Separately, concurrent creation of the same array can race: have one rank call add_array before other ranks begin writing.

docs.title: Combining Icechunk and Sharding
docs.text:
IceChunkBackend does not expose sharding. Instead, pass an Icechunk session's Zarr store to AsyncZarrBackend and manage the transaction yourself:

import icechunk

repo = icechunk.Repository.open_or_create(
    icechunk.local_filesystem_storage("forecast_repo")
)
session = repo.writable_session("main")
io = AsyncZarrBackend(
    "unused",  # Location comes from the store
    parallel_coords=OrderedDict({"time": times, "lead_time": lead_times}),
    shard_coords={"lead_time": 8},
    store=session.store,
)
io.add_array(template)
for forecast in forecasts:
    io.write(forecast)
io.close()  # Finish all writes before committing the external session
session.commit("forecast run")

The same backend can be passed to an Earth2Studio workflow. Wait for close() or flush() to complete before committing; otherwise in-flight writes may be excluded from the snapshot. With this composition, the backend does not commit the external session for you.

docs.title: Cloud Object Storage
docs.text:
Pass store to route writes through a Zarr store rather than fs_factory. URLs and obstore instances use an obstore backed zarr.storage.ObjectStore, with native put and multipart-upload operations:

io = AsyncZarrBackend(
    "unused",
    parallel_coords=OrderedDict({"time": times, "lead_time": lead_times}),
    store="s3://my-bucket/forecasts/run-001.zarr",
    store_kwargs={"region": "us-east-1"},
)

Credentials are resolved from the environment. For explicit store configuration:

from obstore.store import S3Store

io = AsyncZarrBackend(
    "unused",
    parallel_coords=OrderedDict({"time": times, "lead_time": lead_times}),
    store=S3Store("my-bucket", prefix="forecasts/run-001.zarr"),
)

An already constructed Zarr store is also accepted. When store is set, file_name and fs_factory are ignored. Non-blocking writes, sharding, and restart behavior remain the same, with the loop pool sharing one store instance. Close the backend after writing to finish outstanding uploads.

docs.title: Lexicon
docs.text:
As discussed in Data and Metadata section, Earth2Studio tracks the geo-physical representation of tensor data inside workflows. This includes the name of the variable, parameter, and property the data represents, which is tracked explicitly using the Earth2Studios lexicon. Similar to ECMWF's parameter database, Earth2Studio's lexicon aims to provide an opinioned and explicit list of short variables names that is used across the package found in earth2studio.lexicon.base.E2STUDIO_VOCAB. Many of these names are based on ECMWF's parameter database but not all.

Below are a few examples:

  • t2m: Temperature in Kelvin at 2 meters
  • u10m: u-component (eastward/zonal) of winds at 10 meters
  • v10m: v-component (northward/meridional) of winds at 10 meters
  • u200: u-component of winds at 200 hPa
  • z250: Geo-potential at 250 hPa
  • z500: Geo-potential at 500 hPa
  • tcwv: Total column water vapor

Additionally, the lexicon may also be used to track various metadata / coordinate fields. This is particularly relevant for earth2studio.data.base.DataFrameSource where tabular data is used and variables map to the columns of a data frame. Earth2Studio takes a best-effort approach to make these metadata fields standardized across the package.

Some examples include:

  • lat: Latitude coordinate of data, observation, and sensor
  • lon: Longitude coordinate of data, observation, and sensor
  • elev: Elevation (meters) relative to mean sea level of data, observation, and sensor

docs.title: Altitude and Pressure Levels
docs.text:
There are a variety of ways to represent the vertical coordinates for 3D atmospheric variables. The most common method is to slice variables along pressure levels (surfaces of constant pressure), and this is considered the "default" in terms of variable names within the lexicon (for example, z500 is the geo-potential) at the 500 hPa pressure level. Variables which are represented based on altitude above the surface contain an "m" at the end, to denote height in meters, such as u10m.

Some models or workflows, however, require using their own custom vertical coordinate which is neither pressure-level nor terrain-following. These are typically referred to as "native" or "hybrid" vertical levels, and are defined differently for different use-cases. The lexicon supports these custom levels by indexing the vertical level and appending a suffix to the variable name to denote it is a custom vertical level, as in u100k to indicate the u-component of winds at the custom vertical level with index 100 (indexed by k). We leave the choice of suffix up to each use-case, and reserve the following special-case suffixes:

  • No suffix: assumed to be pressure-level, as in z500 for geo-potential at 500 hPa level
  • m: altitude in meters above the surface

Warning

Only use custom vertical level data with caution. The definition of these vertical levels changes with each data source, model, or use-case, and thus they are not necessarily interoperable. Transforming between different custom vertical levels will likely require custom interpolation schemes, possibly using pressure-levels as an intermediate step.

docs.title: Datasource Lexicon
docs.text:
A common challenge when working with different sources of weather and climate data is that variables used may be named or denoted in different ways. The Lexicon is also used to track the translation between Earth2Studios naming scheme and the scheme needed to parse the remote data source. Each remote data store has its own lexicon, which is a dictionary that has the Earth2Studio variable name as the keys and a string used to parse the remote data store. Typically, this value is a string that corresponds to the variable name inside the remote data store.

The following snippet is part of the lexicon for the GFS dataset. The class has a metaclass=LexiconType, which is present in earth2studio.lexicon.base used for type checking.

class GFSLexicon(metaclass=LexiconType):
    """Global Forecast System Lexicon
    GFS specified <Parameter ID>::<Level/ Layer>

    Warning
    -------
    Some variables are only present for lead time greater than 0

    Note
    ----
    Additional resources:
    https://www.nco.ncep.noaa.gov/pmb/products/gfs/gfs.t00z.pgrb2.0p25.f000.shtml
    https://www.nco.ncep.noaa.gov/pmb/products/gfs/gfs.t00z.pgrb2.0p25.f003.shtml
    """

    TIME_STATISTICS: tuple[str, ...] = ("mean", "sum", "min", "max")

    VOCAB = {
        "u10m": "UGRD::10 m above ground",
        "v10m": "VGRD::10 m above ground",
        "u100m": "UGRD::100 m above ground",
        "v100m": "VGRD::100 m above ground",
        "t2m": "TMP::2 m above ground",
        "d2m": "DPT::2 m above ground",
        "r2m": "RH::2 m above ground",
        "q2m": "SPFH::2 m above ground",
        "sp": "PRES::surface",
        "msl": "PRMSL::mean sea level",
        "tcwv": "PWAT::entire atmosphere (considered as a single layer)",
        "tp": "APCP::surface",  # accumulation over the current 6 h bucket; window length grows 1 h to 6 h then restarts
        "tp06": "APCP::surface",  # trailing six-hour total reconstructed by the data source
        "2d": "DPT::2 m above ground",
        "fg10m": "GUST::surface",  # Surface
        "refc": "REFC::entire atmosphere",
        "u1": "UGRD::1 mb",
        "u2": "UGRD::2 mb",
        "u3": "UGRD::3 mb",
        "u5": "UGRD::5 mb",
        "u7": "UGRD::7 mb",
        "u10": "UGRD::10 mb",

Values of each variable is left up to the data source. The present pattern is to split by the string based on the separator ::, and then used to access the required data. For example, the variable u100, zonal winds at 100 hPa, the value UGRD::100 mb is split into UGRD and 100 mb which are then used with the remote Grib index file to fetch the correct data.

        try:
            gfs_name, modifier = GFSLexicon[v]
        except KeyError:
            logger.warning(f"variable id {v} not found in GFS lexicon, good luck")
            gfs_name = v

            def modifier(x: np.array) -> np.array:
                """Modify data (if necessary)."""
                return x

        lead_hour = int(lt.total_seconds() // 3600)
        if v == "tp06":
            # Only a matching six-hour record can satisfy this label directly.
            gfs_name = f"{gfs_name}::{lead_hour - 6}-{lead_hour} hour acc fcst"
        elif v == "tp" and lead_hour > 0:
            # GFS restarts precipitation accumulation every six hours. For
            # leads 1-6, duplicate descriptions resolve to the first (recent
            # accumulation window) record in the index.
            start_hour = 6 * ((lead_hour - 1) // 6)
            gfs_name = f"{gfs_name}::{start_hour}-{lead_hour} hour acc fcst"

        byte_offset = None
        byte_length = None
        for key, value in index_file.items():
            if gfs_name in key:
                byte_offset = value[0]
                byte_length = value[1]
                break

        if byte_length is None or byte_offset is None:
            logger.warning(
                f"Variable {v} not found in index file for time {t} at {lt}, values will be unset"
            )
            return None

It is a common pattern for data source lexicons to contain a modifier function that is used to apply adjustments to align data more uniformly with the package. A good example of this is the GFS dataset which uses the modifier function to transform GFS-supplied geo-potential height to geopotential to better align with other sources inside Earth2Studio.

    @classmethod
    def get_item(cls, val: str) -> tuple[str, Callable]:
        """Get item from GFS vocabulary."""
        gfs_key = cls.VOCAB[val]
        if gfs_key.split("::")[0] == "HGT":

            def mod(x: np.array) -> np.array:
                """Modify data value (if necessary)."""
                return x * 9.81

        elif val in ("tp", "tp06"):

            # TP in GFS is (kg m-2) param id 228228, convert to (m) param id 228
            def mod(x: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
                # Assume density of water is 1000 kg m-3
                # x (kg m-2) / 1000 (kg m-3) = (m)
                return x / 1000.0

        else:

            def mod(x: np.array) -> np.array:
                """Modify data value (if necessary)."""
