                return x

        return gfs_key, mod

Warning

The lexicon does not necessarily contain every variable inside the remote data store. Rather it explicitly lists what is available inside Earth2Studio. Observe a missing variable you would like to add? Open an issue!

docs.title: Deployment and Serving
docs.text:
Earth2Studio is a Python library for building and running weather and climate AI workflows. Deploying those workflows as a service, such as an inference server with a REST API, job queue, object storage, and client, is handled by a separate project: PhysicsNeMo Serve.

For deployment, containers, server configuration, and the client, see the physicsnemo-serve repository and its documentation. Report issues and feature requests for serving and deployment there.

Moved from Earth2Studio

The beta earth2studio.serve package, the serve install extra, and the top-level serve/ directory (server, client, Dockerfile, and example workflows) have been removed from Earth2Studio and now live in PhysicsNeMo Serve. See the migration checklist for details.

docs.title: Core Components
docs.text:
Earth2Studio workflows compose small, interchangeable components. Fetch physical fields, run a model, and pass its labelled outputs to another model, a statistic, or an output backend.

Component Role Data and metadata Describe fields, grids, times, and tabular schemas. Prognostic models Advance a forecast through time. Diagnostic models Derive or transform fields in a single call. Data assimilation models Combine observations and background states. Data sources Fetch gridded fields or tabular observations. Perturbations Generate perturbed fields for ensembles. IO backends Store labelled outputs in memory or on disk. Statistics Reduce fields and compare predictions with observations. Pipelines and runners Run components over many forecasts and stream outputs to storage.

Start with Data and Metadata for the data exchanged between components. See Pipelines and Runners for running them at scale.

Each component page introduces its interface, shows usage, and explains how to implement your own component. Full requirements live in the specifications. You can implement these interfaces in your own project without inheriting a protocol class. For an agent-assisted custom model, start with Wrap Your Own Prognostic Model.

docs.title: Data and Metadata
docs.text:
Creating meaningful data products is a foundation of Earth2Studio. Components produce data, and rich metadata gives those outputs the context that humans and agents need to interpret and use them: what quantities they represent, where and when they apply, and how they were produced.

Earth2Studio uses coordinate systems and metadata structures both to describe existing data and to declare what each component needs and produces. These shared descriptions let people and agents inspect data products, prepare inputs, and connect components into pipelines.

docs.title: Fields and Signatures
docs.text:
Gridded components exchange xarray.DataArray fields with values, named dimensions, coordinate labels, and attributes together. CPU fields typically use NumPy storage; CUDA fields use CuPy. Values cross component boundaries in physical units, with normalization and model-specific preprocessing handled inside the model wrapper.

A CoordinateSystem is a metadata-only DataArray constructed with coord_array. It describes a field without allocating its values; coordinate labels still occupy memory. Models return these signatures from input_coords(), forcing_coords(), and output_coords(...) so callers can plan inputs and output storage before inference.

Member What to inspect .dims Names and order of the field axes. .sizes Length of each axis. .coords Dimension labels and auxiliary coordinates. .dtype Field-value dtype, separate from coordinate dtypes. .attrs Grid, temporal-statistics, and descriptive metadata.

Inspect signature metadata rather than .values, which is unsupported for these allocation-free objects. An execution field contains real values accessible through .data. The legacy CoordSystem mapping does not capture the full metadata interface.

docs.title: Dimensions and Time
docs.text:
Coordinate dtypes describe labels independently of the field-value dtype.

Name Coordinate dtype Meaning time NumPy datetime64 Absolute time; forecast reference time when paired with leads. lead_time NumPy timedelta64 Offset from reference time, including input history. valid_time NumPy datetime64 Auxiliary valid time; time + lead_time for forecasts. variable String labels Physical quantity identifiers, including temporal qualifiers. ensemble Declared dtype, often integer or string Member identity, not array position. batch Declared label dtype, if labelled Independent samples; may be unlabelled. lat, lon Floating-point Geographic coordinates in degrees, as axes or auxiliaries. y, x Numeric or integer indexes Native spatial coordinates or grid indexes. hpx, face, height, width Integer indexes HEALPix pixel or layout indexes.

Use NumPy datetime64 for absolute times and timedelta64 for offsets. For example, an initialization at 00 UTC with a six-hour lead is valid at 06 UTC. A history window with leads [-6h, 0h] describes two input frames relative to the reference time.

Dynamic dimensions are an explicitly declared, zero-sized leading prefix in a signature. A model can accept concrete leading axes such as time and ensemble through that prefix; its remaining dimensions still describe the fixed input layout. See Batch Dimension for batching patterns.

Time labels locate a field, while a temporal qualifier describes the quantity over a window. For example, tp:sum:6h identifies a six-hour accumulation ending at the target time. Coordinate constructors derive earth2studio_statistics metadata from qualified labels. See E2S-03: Time Statistics for window syntax, source support, and calendar-day semantics.

docs.title: Spatial Grids
docs.text:
A GridDefinition describes geometry independently of field values or interpolation. Its dims and shape describe spatial axes, coords() supplies coordinates, and crs identifies the native coordinate reference system where applicable. topology, serializable attrs, and fingerprint() describe the grid family and identity. subset_indexers() supports spatial selection; cell_bounds() supplies cell geometry when available.

Definition Typical dimensions Geometry LatLonGrid lat, lon Rectilinear geographic axes. ProjectedGrid y, x Native projected coordinates with a CRS. CurvilinearGrid y, x Two-dimensional latitude and longitude auxiliaries. PointGrid x Individual geographic sample locations. HEALPixGrid hpx or face, height, width Explicit pixel ordering and layout.

Pass a grid object or registered name to coord_array to attach its geometry. infer_grid(signature) recovers a target grid for fetching or regridding. Matching array shapes alone does not establish matching geography: axis order, CRS, and HEALPix ordering can differ.

docs.title: Attributes and Tabular Schemas
docs.text:
Grid metadata includes geometry descriptions, earth2studio_crs, and, for registered grids, earth2studio_grid_id. Descriptive attributes can record units and provenance. For a mixed-variable field, describe units per variable rather than assigning one field-level unit to quantities with different meanings.

Sparse observations use pandas or cuDF DataFrames. A model's FrameSchema maps column names to NumPy arrays describing dtype and allowed values: an empty array leaves values unconstrained, while a nonempty array lists allowed values. These are column declarations, not example rows. A source's PyArrow SCHEMA instead describes available column types, nullability, and field metadata. See Tabular Observations for fetching them.

docs.title: Standard DataFrame Fields
docs.text:
These fields form a shared vocabulary, not a requirement to include every column. The source's SCHEMA and the consuming model's FrameSchema determine which fields are available and required. Types below are the suggested PyArrow types from E2STUDIO_SCHEMA; check the source schema for its exact types and nullability. The units of observation depend on variable.

Name Suggested Arrow type Meaning time timestamp[ns] Observation time or forecast reference time, in UTC. lat float32 Latitude in degrees, within [-90, 90]. lon float32 Longitude in degrees, within [0, 360]. elev float32 Observation elevation above the surface, metres. observation float32 Measurement or predicted value of the identified variable. variable string Earth2Studio quantity identifier. pres float32 Observation pressure level, Pa. type, class string Observation type identifier and class. source, station string Per-row source and station identifiers. station_elev float32 Station elevation, metres. quality uint16 Quality-control marker; 0 is best, 15 is missing. satellite string Satellite platform identifier. scan_angle float32 Satellite scan angle, degrees. sensor_index uint16 Sensor channel index. solza, solaza float32 Solar zenith and azimuth angles, degrees. satellite_za, satellite_aza float32 Satellite zenith and azimuth angles, degrees. wavenumber float64 Channel wavenumber, cm^-1. track_id, storm_name, basin string Track identifier, storm name, and basin code. season int32 Tropical cyclone season year.

Forecast frames can also declare lead_time as an Arrow duration and valid_time as a timestamp equal to time + lead_time. A DataFrame's row index does not replace its time, location, or variable columns.

Full contracts are defined in E2S-01: Core Metadata, E2S-02: Grids, and E2S-03: Time Statistics.

docs.title: Declare and Inspect a Field
docs.text:
Create a small grid-backed signature with two history frames:

import numpy as np

from earth2studio.grids import LatLonGrid, infer_grid
from earth2studio.utils import coord_array

grid = LatLonGrid(
    np.array([50.0, 49.0, 48.0]),
    np.array([0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0]),
)
signature = coord_array(
    ("batch", "lead_time", "variable", "lat", "lon"),
    {
        "lead_time": np.array([-6, 0], dtype="timedelta64[h]"),
        "variable": ["t2m"],
    },
    dynamic=("batch",),
    grid=grid,
)
print(signature.dims)
print(signature.sizes)
target_grid = infer_grid(signature)

For a loaded model, inspect model.input_coords() the same way. Pass the recovered grid to fetch_data(..., target_grid=target_grid) to prepare matching inputs; Data Sources shows the complete request.

A concrete field on this grid carries actual values:

import xarray as xr

field = xr.DataArray(
    np.full(grid.shape, 280.0, dtype=np.float32),
    dims=grid.dims,
    coords=grid.coords(),
    name="t2m",
    attrs={**grid.attrs, "units": "K", "source": "local-example"},
)

docs.title: Preserve Meaning Across Transformations
docs.text:
Use coord_array_like to derive an output signature when retaining an input's geometry. For a new spatial domain, build a new grid-backed signature so the metadata describes the actual crop or transformed grid. After reordering spatial axes on registered-grid data, remove the stale earth2studio_grid_id so grid inference uses the actual coordinates; see the grid specification's current reconstruction guidance.

PyTorch wrappers convert at their computation boundary with field.e2s.to_torch() and restore labelled fields with from_torch(tensor, output_signature). Public component handoffs remain DataArrays. Signature-only markers are not field metadata; the conversion helpers handle that distinction.

docs.title: Shared CUDA Memory
docs.text:
On Linux CUDA systems with RMM installed, the auto and cupy backends share memory pools between Torch, CuPy, and cuDF while preserving existing custom RMM resources. Import Earth2Studio or select the CuPy backend before initializing Torch CUDA. Set EARTH2STUDIO_DISABLE_RMM=1 before import to retain existing allocators. Non-Linux systems, missing RMM, CPU-only imports, and initial numpy or torch backends skip this setup.

RMM's Torch adapter does not honor Tensor.record_stream(): keep tensors alive until their streams finish, or disable RMM. Use RMM instrumentation for pool statistics; Torch's native cache controls do not manage these shared pools.

docs.title: Describe Your Own Component
docs.text:
Start with your inference inputs and outputs: name the axes, variables and units, history and forecast times, and spatial grid. Declare these with coord_array and use them in the component's coordinate methods. Document any custom labels or axes so other components and agents can interpret them.

Reuse a built-in grid definition where possible. For a new geometry, implement the GridDefinition interface and optionally register it with register_grid for reuse. For tabular inputs, declare the needed columns and value constraints in a FrameSchema. Check your declarations against a representative field or observation batch before connecting the component to a pipeline.

The custom prognostic wrapper guide shows how to give these details to an agent along with your inference code and reference predictions.

docs.title: Data Assimilation Models
docs.text:
Earth2Studio's data assimilation interface supports models that ingest, predict, and assimilate sparse observations. Traditional assimilation combines observations with an optional background field to produce an updated state. The same interface also supports predicting observations directly from other observations, without requiring a gridded analysis as an intermediate output.

Use these models to prepare initial conditions, update forecasts with new measurements, or produce observation-space predictions. The assimilation API supports both independent calls and models that continue a stateful trajectory.

docs.title: Interface
docs.text:
Method Purpose input_coords() Declare initial inputs, including observations for independent models. output_coords(...) Validate input declarations and plan the output. default_sources() Recommend providers in input-then-forcing order. model(...) Produce an analysis or prediction from separate, named inputs. to(device) Place model computation on the requested device.

AssimilationModel defines this independent interface. StatefulAssimilationModel adds forcing_coords(), initialize(...), step(..., state=state), and create_iterator(...), following the prognostic explicit-state convention. For these models, observations supplied during a rollout are forcing. The protocols are in earth2studio.models.da.base; inheritance is optional.

Each input or output slot is either a gridded DataArray described by a CoordinateSystem, or a DataFrame described by a FrameSchema. A schema maps column names to representative NumPy arrays: empty arrays leave values unconstrained; nonempty arrays specify allowed values. Multiple slots form an ordered tuple, which can mix gridded and tabular declarations. Models expose stochastic and set_rng; seeding is a no-op for deterministic models.

For an observation-to-observation model, input and output FrameSchema declarations describe the observations consumed and predicted. Neither side requires a gridded field; choose the slot types that match the model's actual inputs and outputs.

See E2S-07: Data Assimilation Contract for slot ordering, observation schemas and timing, and independent and stateful execution requirements.

docs.title: Choose the Execution Pattern
docs.text:
Model Inputs Forcing Execution InterpEquirectangular Observations — Independent HealDA Conventional, satellite observations — Independent CorrDiffCosmoEra5SDA ERA5 background, observations — Independent StormCastSDA HRRR background Conditioning, observations Independent or stateful StormCastConusSDA HRRR background Conditioning, observations Independent or stateful

For example, load HealDA through its concrete class, with its optional dependencies and weights installed. Given observation frames prepared to match its two schemas:

from earth2studio.models.da import HealDA

model = HealDA.load_model(HealDA.load_default_package())
analysis = model(conv_obs, sat_obs)

HealDA requires at least one observation batch. CorrDiff accepts model(background, observations), where observations may be None. Use fetch_dataframe and fetch_dataframes to prepare observation requests and retain request-time metadata.

docs.title: Continue a Stateful Analysis
docs.text:
For a loaded StormCastSDA model and prepared fields:

analysis, state = model.initialize(x0, conditioning0, obs0)
analysis, state = model.step(analysis, conditioning1, None, state=state)

Or let the iterator retain state:

iterator = model.create_iterator(x0, conditioning0, obs0)
analysis = next(iterator)  # First computed analysis, one hour after x0
analysis = iterator.send((conditioning1, None))  # Next step without observations
iterator.close()

Conditioning remains required when observations are absent: next(iterator) or send(None) cannot replace send((conditioning, None)). StormCastSDA aligns conditioning to the input valid time and observations to the output time, one hour later. StormCastConusSDA aligns both to the output valid time and filters observations using the wrapped model's time_tolerance.

docs.title: Wrap Your Own Assimilation Model
docs.text:
Keep a wrapper in your own project. Declare gridded signatures and observation schemas, use fixed named execution arguments, and implement the stateful extension only when outputs and explicit state continue a trajectory. Validate observation timing and optional-input behavior as well as numerical agreement with your reference analysis or observation predictions.

The earth2studio-create-assimilation skill provides contract and validation guidance. Ask your agent to adapt it to a local wrapper, supplying your inference code, observation schema, background/forcing requirements, and reference cases. See the prognostic customization guide for an example agent request scoped to your project.

docs.title: Data and Forecast Sources
docs.text: Sources fetch weather and climate data from remote services or local files. They provide initial conditions, conditioning fields, observations, and verification targets. Browse the analysis, forecast, and tabular source APIs.

docs.title: Interface
docs.text:
Source Call Output DataSource source(time, variable) DataArray: time, variable, ... ForecastSource source(time, lead_time, variable) Forecast DataArray DataFrameSource source(time, variable, fields=None) Observation DataFrame ForecastFrameSource source(time, lead_time, variable, fields=None) DataFrame

Forecast DataArrays have dimensions time, lead_time, variable, .... Forecast time is the initialization time; lead_time selects offsets from that initialization. Analysis time selects valid times directly. Tabular sources expose SCHEMA; fields selects observation columns. The protocols are in earth2studio.data.base. Some sources also offer an async fetch with equivalent arguments and results.

docs.title: Ensemble Members
docs.text:
EnsembleDataSource and EnsembleForecastSource add a member keyword. It selects source-native member labels and returns a leading ensemble dimension, including for a single requested member. Omitting it returns the source's configured member without adding that dimension.

See E2S-05: Data Fetching for request handling, output assembly, ensemble selection, and device-placement requirements.

docs.title: Fetch Gridded Fields
docs.text:
fetch_data assembles a field with dimensions time, lead_time, variable, ..., optionally preceded by ensemble. It accepts both analysis and forecast sources: analysis sources are queried at time + lead_time, while forecast sources retain their initialization cycle. Floating values are converted to float32.

Choose variable names and physical units using the source's lexicon. Set device on the source constructor to choose where it returns data; fetch_data can then move gridded fields to the model's execution device.

import numpy as np

from earth2studio.data import GFS, fetch_data

times = np.array(["2024-01-01T00"], dtype="datetime64[ns]")
variables = np.array(["t2m", "u10m", "v10m"])
field = fetch_data(
    GFS(), times, variables,
    lead_time=np.array([0], dtype="timedelta64[h]"),
    device="cpu",
)

Use nonempty, one-dimensional datetime and timedelta arrays with finite labels. The result is a field DataArray: access values through .data and coordinates through .coords. Remote sources commonly cache downloads; see Configuration.

docs.title: Match a Model Grid
docs.text:
For a single-input model, request its declared variables, history, and geometry:

from earth2studio.grids import infer_grid

signature = model.input_coords()
x = fetch_data(
    GFS(), times, signature.coords["variable"].values,
    lead_time=signature.coords["lead_time"].values,
    target_grid=infer_grid(signature),
    device="cuda:0",
)

Matching grids pass through; exact crops are selected. Otherwise target_grid uses nearest-neighbor regridding and rejects targets outside source coverage. For repeated requests or another method, build a compatible regridder once and pass regridder=...; list_regridders(source_grid, target_grid) lists available methods. Temporal reductions happen on the source grid, followed by device placement and regridding.

RegriddedSource combines a source and reusable regridder. CompositeSource joins analysis sources supplying different variables on a shared grid; CompositeForecastSource also supports forecast sources.

docs.title: Temporal Statistics
docs.text:
For a source supporting the requested statistic:

field = fetch_data(source, times, np.array(["t2m:mean:24h"]))

Windows are left-open and right-closed: a six-hourly source includes samples at T-18h, T-12h, T-6h, and T for a 24-hour mean ending at T. NaN samples propagate. Forecast windows must stay within the requested initialization's available leads. Summing stored accumulations with overlapping windows can double-count totals; check the source's temporal-statistics documentation. The output's earth2studio_statistics metadata describes the reduction performed. See E2S-03: Time Statistics for label syntax, supported sources, and calendar-day windows.

docs.title: Tabular Observations
docs.text:
fetch_dataframe fetches requested variables and fields and records attrs["request_time"] for assimilation models. fetch_dataframes makes multiple requests concurrently. For a model whose inputs are all observation schemas:

from earth2studio.data import fetch_dataframes

schemas = model.input_coords()
observations = fetch_dataframes(list(zip(sources, schemas)), times)
analysis = model(*observations)

Each (source, schema) pair uses the schema's variable entry for variables and other keys for fields. A list returns frames in the same order; a dictionary of named requests returns a dictionary. Prepare mixed gridded/tabular slots separately.

docs.title: Create Your Own Source
docs.text:
Wrap a local dataset or service in a callable that follows the appropriate source interface. Translate variable names and units, preserve request order and grid metadata, and report unsupported times or variables explicitly. Accept device in the constructor and expose the configured device on the instance.

The earth2studio-create-datasource skill provides templates for all four source types. Ask your agent to create a wrapper in your project, using sample files or service responses to verify indexing, units, coordinates, and device placement. See the extension examples.

docs.title: Diagnostic Models
docs.text: Diagnostic models transform physical fields in a single call: for example, deriving precipitation, downscaling a forecast, or generating samples conditioned on a state. They do not continue an autoregressive trajectory. Browse the diagnostic API for available models.

docs.title: Interface
docs.text:
Method Purpose input_coords() Declare one input signature or an ordered tuple of signatures. output_coords(...) Validate input coordinates and declare the output signatures. default_sources() Recommend providers in input-slot order. model(x) Transform a field; multiple inputs are separate named arguments. to(device) Place model computation on the requested device.

Fields are xarray.DataArray objects; signatures follow the Data and Metadata. Return one output directly or multiple outputs as a tuple. The protocol is earth2studio.models.dx.base.DiagnosticModel; inheritance is optional. The stochastic flag and, for stochastic models, set_rng(seed, reset=True) describe randomness. Diagnostic models require no forcing, state, iterator, or hook interface.

See E2S-06: Model Contract for diagnostic-model requirements, including coordinate planning, output ownership, randomness, and optional domain selection.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
Load pretrained models through their concrete class, for example:

from earth2studio.models.dx import PrecipitationAFNO

model = PrecipitationAFNO.load_model(PrecipitationAFNO.load_default_package())
model = model.to("cuda:0")

This requires the model's optional dependencies and weights; see AutoModels. Given a field x prepared on the model's device with the required variables and grid:

planned = model.output_coords(x)  # Validate and inspect output coordinates
precipitation = model(x)

When chaining models, inspect the diagnostic's input_coords() and explicitly select or regrid the prognostic output to match it. A common grid does not guarantee matching variable order, history, or accumulation windows.

docs.title: Wrap Your Own Diagnostic Model
docs.text:
Implement the interface in a local module, with fixed named arguments such as __call__(self, atmosphere, ocean). Use coord_array for declarations and coord_array_like when preserving an input's geometry. For PyTorch computation, convert at the boundary with .e2s.to_torch() and from_torch().

The earth2studio-create-diagnostic skill includes wrapper and validation guidance. Ask your agent to adapt it to a standalone wrapper in your project, supplying your inference script, weights, variable/unit definitions, and input/output grids. Validate against reference predictions as well as the declared interface. The prognostic customization guide shows how to scope an agent request to local use.

docs.title: Pipelines and Runners
docs.text:
Execution tools in earth2studio.run make it easy to run workflows composing multiple components (models, data sources, etc.) over many dates and ensemble members. This is done using three core layers, from smallest to largest:

  • A WorkItem identifies one forecast to produce: an initialization time, a final lead time, and optional ensemble members. An inference campaign usually spans many different work items.
  • A Runner defines what is run for each work item. It holds the models and data sources and specifies how an item's inputs are fetched, how models are stepped, and what streams of output data are produced.
  • A Pipeline executes the Runner over many work items. It acts as an orchestrator: distributing items across ranks, selecting and regridding outputs, writing each output stream to storage, and potentially resuming interrupted runs or scoring the outputs as they're produced.

Changing what a forecast produces means choosing or writing a Runner; changing how and where forecasts run means configuring the Pipeline. Models can also be called directly (see Prognostic Models); Pipeline execution is best suited for more complex workflows and larger inference campaigns run at scale.

docs.title: Work Items
docs.text:
A WorkItem describes one forecast: a reference time, a final_lead_time, and optional ensemble member_ids. Build items with work_items:

import numpy as np

from earth2studio.run import work_items

times = [np.datetime64("2024-01-01T00"), np.datetime64("2024-01-02T00")]
items = work_items(times, final_lead_time=np.timedelta64(240, "h"))
ensemble = work_items(
    times, final_lead_time=np.timedelta64(240, "h"), members=8, member_batch=4
)

member_batch sets how many members each item runs together. Each item produces lead times from zero through its final lead time, which must be a multiple of the model's step.

docs.title: Runners
docs.text:
A Runner defines the core execution loop for a WorkItem and declares its inputs (data fetches) and outputs (prediction fields). Runners group outputs into distinct streams: each stream is a named sequence of outputs with one set of variables, one grid, and one lead-time pattern.

Member Purpose supports_member_batching Whether one item may carry several members. to(device) Place models on a device, and fetch inputs onto it. output_coords(final_lead_time) Declare each stream's output signature without running. data_requests(item) Describe every fetch an item will make, or None if not known upfront. run_item(item) Yield one mapping per step, from stream name to output field.

A runner is built once with its models and sources, then reused for every item; data is fetched, from live or predownloaded sources, inside run_item.

The built-in runners are:

  • PrognosticRunner rolls out one prognostic model, yielding the forecast stream. Each diagnostic in diagnostics adds a stream under its key. It accepts an optional perturbation for initial-condition ensembles.
  • DiagnosticRunner applies diagnostics directly to source data. Step k reads the source at the item's time plus k * step.
  • CoupledRunner (earth2studio.coupling) runs several models together; see Coupled Models.

Sources default to each model's default_sources(). The protocol is defined in earth2studio.run.runner.Runner; inheritance is not required.

docs.title: Pipeline
docs.text:
A Pipeline provides the outer orchestration layer around a Runner, managing distributed execution of work items, tracking progress, and writing each output stream to its store.

Argument Purpose runner Runner executing each item. output IO backend per stream; streams left out are not written. output_variables Variables kept per stream. regridder Regridder per stream, applied after variable selection. scorer Online scoring hook, called with each output before it is written. progress ProgressStore recording finished items so a rerun resumes. device Runner device; "auto" selects cuda:{LOCAL_RANK} or CPU.

At least one of output and scorer is required.

Construct a Pipeline explicitly from a Runner and per-stream settings, or use Pipeline.from_model(model, source, ...) to build one for a single prognostic model, as shown below.

See E2S-11: Execution Contracts for the full work item, runner, pipeline, seeding, and progress requirements.

docs.title: Run a Forecast
docs.text:
Given a loaded prognostic model, from_model runs it from a data source and writes the forecast stream:

from earth2studio.data import GFS
from earth2studio.io import ZarrBackend
from earth2studio.run import Pipeline

Pipeline.from_model(
    model,
    GFS(),
    output={"forecast": ZarrBackend("forecast.zarr")},
    output_variables={"forecast": ["t2m", "u10m", "v10m"]},
).run(items)

The store is planned from all items before any runs, so its time axis spans every initialization. The initial condition is written at lead time zero when the model's outputs include its inputs. Pass ensemble items to write a store with an ensemble dimension.

docs.title: Add Diagnostics or Use a Runner Directly
docs.text:
Each diagnostic yields its own stream, written to its own backend:

from earth2studio.models.dx import PrecipitationAFNO
from earth2studio.perturbation import Gaussian
from earth2studio.run import PrognosticRunner

precip = PrecipitationAFNO.load_model(PrecipitationAFNO.load_default_package())
runner = PrognosticRunner(
    model,
    GFS(),
    diagnostics={"precip": precip},
    perturbation=Gaussian(noise_amplitude=0.05),
)
Pipeline(
    runner,
    output={"forecast": forecast_io, "precip": precip_io},
).run(ensemble)

Each member's perturbation is seeded from the runner's seed, the item time, and the member ID, so results are reproducible regardless of how members are batched. Stochastic models are seeded once per item; use member_batch=1 to reproduce each member independently.

Runners can also be used on their own, without Pipeline:

for step in runner.run_item(items[0]):
    print(step["forecast"].lead_time.values)

docs.title: Resume and Distribute
docs.text:
A ProgressStore marks an item done once its outputs are flushed. Running the same items again skips finished ones:

from earth2studio.run import ProgressStore

progress = ProgressStore("out/.progress", tags={"model": "SFNO"})
Pipeline.from_model(model, GFS(), output=output, progress=progress).run(items)

The store refuses to resume a run whose stream layout, seed, member grouping, or tags differ. It cannot tell models apart, so record the model and checkpoint in tags. An interrupted item reruns in full.

For multi-GPU runs, launch the script with torchrun and initialize a process group before calling run. Each rank runs a contiguous slice of the remaining items, and rank 0 creates the stores. Build backends on every rank, letting rank 0 create storage first:

from earth2studio.run.work import rank0_first

output = rank0_first(lambda: {"forecast": ZarrBackend("out/forecast.zarr")})

Distributed stores must use chunks of 1 along time and ensemble, which is the ZarrBackend default; Pipeline checks this before running.

docs.title: Coupled Models
docs.text:
CoupledRunner runs several models as named components. Connector declarations describe which component feeds another's inputs, including variable mapping, time selection, and optional regridding. Each component runs at its own cadence and writes its own stream; inputs not fed by a connector are fetched from sources.

Because CoupledRunner is a runner, the same Pipeline drives it. For example, DLESyM's atmosphere and ocean each advance in 96-hour cycles, publishing outputs every 6 and 48 hours respectively. The final lead time must be a multiple of the 96-hour cycle:

from earth2studio.coupling import Connector, CoupledRunner

runner = CoupledRunner(
    {"atmos": atmos, "ocean": ocean},
    [
        Connector("ocean", "atmos", time="hold"),  # Latest SST before each cycle
        Connector("atmos", "ocean"),               # Atmospheric means per ocean step
    ],
)
final_lead_time = np.timedelta64(192, "h")  # Two coupled cycles
print(runner.describe(final_lead_time))  # Inspect the derived schedule
coupled_items = work_items(times, final_lead_time=final_lead_time)
Pipeline(runner, output={"atmos": atmos_io, "ocean": ocean_io}).run(coupled_items)

See E2S-12: Coupling for connector and scheduling requirements, and the DLESyM seasonal example for a complete coupled run.

docs.title: Write Your Own Runner
docs.text: Any object with the runner members above works with Pipeline. Wrap a built-in runner to change its behavior, such as stopping a rollout early, or write one for a workflow the built-ins do not cover. Keep stream names stable across items and runs, since they key output stores and resume. Declare every stream in output_coords, and give outputs with different grids or cadences separate streams. Return None from data_requests when fetches depend on results.

docs.title: Output Handling
docs.text:
IO backends store the labelled DataArrays produced by workflows. AsyncZarrBackend is a good general-purpose default, supporting asynchronous and sharded writes. Use ZarrBackend for synchronous Zarr output, NetCDF4Backend for netCDF files, XarrayBackend for in-memory results, or IceChunkBackend for versioned output. See the IO API for backend options.

For Icechunk transactions, asynchronous writes, sharding, and cloud storage, see Advanced Output Handling.

docs.title: Interface
docs.text:
Method Purpose add_array(template) Create arrays from dimensions, coordinates, dtype, and metadata. write(x) Store values at positions identified by the field's coordinate labels. flush() Wait for pending writes to become visible to readers. close() Flush, finalize the store, and release resources.

The earth2studio.io.base.IOBackend protocol requires these four methods; inheritance is optional. Reading and dictionary-like access are backend-specific capabilities rather than requirements of the write interface.

See E2S-10: IO for template, label-based writing, metadata, and lifecycle requirements.

docs.title: Declare and Write a Forecast
docs.text:
Given a loaded single-input, unforced model and prepared initial field x, plan a store for the full output horizon. Here times contains the initialization times in x, and lead_times contains all forecast leads you will write:

from itertools import islice

from earth2studio.io import AsyncZarrBackend
from earth2studio.io.utils import output_template

io = AsyncZarrBackend(
    "forecast.zarr",
    parallel_coords={"time": times, "lead_time": lead_times},
)
signature = model.output_coords(model.input_coords())
template = output_template(
    signature,
    leading={"time": times},  # Resolve the dynamic leading batch prefix
    coords={"lead_time": lead_times},
)
io.add_array(template)

iterator = model.create_iterator(x)
try:
    for y in islice(iterator, nsteps):
        io.write(y)
finally:
    iterator.close()
    io.close()

The iterator writes forecasts only. If you also store the initial condition, include its lead time in the template and write the appropriately selected field separately. For chunk-producing models, each write may contain multiple forecast leads.

parallel_coords declares the labels along axes that can be written independently. Here, writes can select initialization times and forecast leads; each write covers the full extent of other dimensions. Add any other independently written axes, such as ensemble, to parallel_coords.

Close the backend when the workflow finishes; earth2studio.run does not close it for you. With Icechunk, flush exposes pending writes within the open transaction, while close commits the output.

docs.title: Read Results
docs.text:
Backends with read, such as XarrayBackend, accept a template or a mapping from every dimension to the requested labels:

from earth2studio.io import XarrayBackend

memory = XarrayBackend()
memory.add_array(y)
memory.write(y)
field = memory.read(y)
memory.close()

Pass device="cuda:0" for a CuPy-backed result where supported. Stored formats can also be opened directly with Xarray, for example:

import xarray as xr

dataset = xr.open_zarr("forecast.zarr")

docs.title: Create Your Own Backend
docs.text: Implement the four methods in a local class. Validate templates and writes before modifying storage, preserve coordinate and grid metadata, and make flush and close reflect your storage system's visibility and durability guarantees. Reading is optional; clearly document any restrictions on partial writes or concurrency.

docs.title: Perturbations
docs.text: Perturbations generate alternative initial conditions for ensemble forecasts, from simple Gaussian noise to spatially correlated noise and bred vectors. Browse the perturbation API for available methods.

docs.title: Interface
docs.text:
perturbed = perturbation(x)  # DataArray -> DataArray

A perturbation accepts a field and returns the perturbed field, not just noise. The earth2studio.perturbation.base.Perturbation protocol requires only this call; inheritance is optional. Built-in methods accept NumPy-, CuPy-, or Torch-backed DataArrays and use PyTorch for computation.

See E2S-08: Perturbations for field preservation, method-specific dimensions, and backend behavior.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
Given a t2m field x in kelvin, construct four members with independent noise:

import numpy as np

from earth2studio.perturbation import Gaussian

ensemble = x.expand_dims(ensemble=np.arange(4))
perturbation = Gaussian(noise_amplitude=0.1, seed=42)  # 0.1 K for this field
perturbed = perturbation(ensemble)

Gaussian uses a private random generator: pass seed for reproducible runs, or call perturbation.set_rng(42) to restart its stream. torch.manual_seed does not control every perturbation; check the selected method's seeding interface.

Choose amplitudes in the field's physical units. For multiple variables, a broadcastable tensor can assign a different scale to each variable. Check the selected method's grid and dimension requirements before applying it; Gaussian does not impose a spatial layout.

The built-in earth2studio.run.ensemble workflow expands the ensemble dimension and applies the perturbation once to the initial input. For bred vectors, provide a model-like callable accepting and returning DataArrays; see the method's API for its integration and rescaling options.

docs.title: Create Your Own Perturbation
docs.text:
Implement a callable in your own project. For example, a multiplicative perturbation can preserve metadata and leave its input untouched:

import xarray as xr


class Scale:
    def __init__(self, factor: float):
        self.factor = factor

    def __call__(self, x: xr.DataArray) -> xr.DataArray:
        return x.copy(data=x.data * self.factor)

Check that your method preserves coordinates and attributes, does not modify its input, and produces the intended amplitude in physical units. See the extension examples for workflow integrations.

docs.title: Prognostic Models
docs.text: Prognostic models advance atmospheric or other physical fields through time. A model can produce one forecast chunk or continue a trajectory using explicit state. Browse the built-in models in the prognostic API.

docs.title: Interface
docs.text:
Models exchange labelled xarray.DataArray fields in physical units. Coordinate methods describe those fields without allocating their values; see the Data and Metadata.

For a model with one input and no forcing, the interface is:

Method Purpose input_coords() Declare initial fields, history, variables, and grid. forcing_coords() Declare external conditioning; None when unforced. output_coords(input_coords) Validate coordinates and plan the output. default_sources() Recommend data providers for the caller. model(x) Compute an independent forecast chunk. initialize(x) Return the first forecast and continuation state: (y, state). step(y, state=state) Return the next forecast and updated state. create_iterator(x) Manage state internally and yield forecast chunks. to(device) Place model computation on the requested device.

Multi-input models take separate, named arguments in declared order. Forcing follows the initial inputs in initialize and the previous outputs in step, with state last. One output is returned directly; multiple outputs form an ordered tuple. The protocol is defined in earth2studio.models.px.base.PrognosticModel; inheritance from it is not required. stochastic identifies stochastic models, which expose set_rng(seed, reset=True) for reproducible rollouts.

See E2S-06: Model Contract for the full coordinate, execution, state, randomness, and domain-selection requirements.

docs.title: Load and Predict
docs.text:
Use a concrete model class to load pretrained weights. This example requires SFNO's optional dependencies, weights, and sufficient device memory; see AutoModels.

import numpy as np

from earth2studio.data import GFS, fetch_data
from earth2studio.grids import infer_grid
from earth2studio.models.px import SFNO

device = "cuda:0"
model = SFNO.load_model(SFNO.load_default_package()).to(device)
signature = model.input_coords()
x = fetch_data(
    GFS(),
    np.array(["2024-01-01T00"], dtype="datetime64[ns]"),
    signature.coords["variable"].values,
    lead_time=signature.coords["lead_time"].values,
    device=device,
    target_grid=infer_grid(signature),
)
planned = model.output_coords(x)  # Coordinate validation, without inference
y = model(x)

docs.title: Continue a Forecast
docs.text:
Use explicit state when you need to save or branch a trajectory:

y, state = model.initialize(x)             # First forecast
y, state = model.step(y, state=state)      # Second forecast

For a simple unforced rollout, use the iterator instead:

from itertools import islice

iterator = model.create_iterator(x)
for y in islice(iterator, 4):
    print(y.lead_time.values)  # SFNO: 6h, 12h, 18h, 24h
iterator.close()

For forced models, pass the initial forcing window to create_iterator, then use iterator.send(forcing) for each subsequent step, or send a tuple for multiple forcing slots. Supply the newest required frames; required time-varying forcing is not fetched or silently reused. Static forcing without a lead_time dimension is supplied only at initialization.

PrognosticMixin provides iterator hooks: rear_hook runs before every yield, including the first, and front_hook runs before subsequent steps. Both affect the continuing trajectory. Hooks do not run in model(x), initialize, or step; perturb the initial input explicitly when needed. For stochastic models, call set_rng before a new rollout; reseeding does not change an existing explicit state.

docs.title: Wrap Your Own Prognostic Model
docs.text:
Keep a wrapper in your own project, such as my_project/models/my_model.py, and pass its instance to Earth2Studio workflows just like a built-in model. The wrapper adapts your existing inference code to the interface above, handling coordinates, physical-unit conversion, device placement, and explicit continuation state.

The earth2studio-create-prognostic agentic skill provides a model contract, wrapper skeleton, method templates, and validation guidance. Give your coding agent the skill directory from a checkout matching your Earth2Studio version, and ask it to load SKILL.md and the referenced files. Provide:

  • Your working inference script, weights, configuration, and dependency requirements.
  • Input/output variable names and units, grid, normalization, history, and forecast step.
  • Required forcing or static data, device support, and stochastic behavior.
  • A small reference input and expected output for numerical comparison.

For example:

Use the earth2studio-create-prognostic skill to wrap my existing model in
my_project/models/my_model.py for local use with Earth2Studio. Follow the model
contract and relevant rules from this checkout. Scope the work to my project;
skip package exports, dependency extras, changelog, and pull-request steps.

Reference inference: <script>; weights/configuration: <paths>.
Variables/units/grid: <details>; history and forecast step: <details>.
Forcing, normalization, devices, and randomness: <details>.

Preserve the reference inference behavior. Validate coordinate-only planning,
single-call and multi-step execution, input immutability, state replay, and
numerical agreement with the reference. Show a short local usage example.

Use explicit named parameters for every input and forcing slot. Build signatures with coord_array and coord_array_like; for PyTorch models, use x.e2s.to_torch() and from_torch() at field boundaries. PrognosticMixin supplies private call/iterator helpers, but your wrapper must expose its public methods. Automatic weight downloading is optional: a wrapper can accept an already loaded model and local assets.

The skill's conformance checks help validate the interface. Also compare a short rollout with your reference implementation: matching shapes alone does not establish that normalization, timing, or predictions are correct. See the extension examples for complete integrations.

docs.title: Statistics and Metrics
docs.text: Statistics summarize a field, such as its mean or variance. Metrics compare a prediction with observations, such as root-mean-square error (RMSE) or continuous ranked probability score (CRPS). Browse the statistics API for available operations.

docs.title: Interface
docs.text:
Member Statistic Metric reduction_dimensions Names of dimensions to reduce Names of dimensions to reduce output_coords(x) Plan from the input signature Plan from the forecast signature __call__(...) statistic(x) metric(x, y)

Inputs and outputs are DataArrays. Coordinate planning uses allocation-free signatures; see Data and Metadata. The Statistic and Metric protocols live in earth2studio.statistics.base; inheritance is optional. Weights, streaming updates, and ensemble handling are options of particular implementations rather than universal requirements.

See E2S-09: Statistics for dimension handling, input alignment, weights, streaming state, and backend requirements.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
First align forecast and observation labels and grids; metrics do not interpolate or implicitly align coordinates. For fields with lat and lon dimensions:

from earth2studio.statistics import mean, rmse

spatial_mean = mean(["lat", "lon"])
average = spatial_mean(forecast)

error = rmse(["lat", "lon"])
planned = error.output_coords(forecast)
score = error(forecast, observations)

For a regular latitude-longitude grid ordered ..., lat, lon, cosine-latitude weights give an area-weighted mean:

import numpy as np

lat = forecast.coords["lat"].values
weights = np.cos(np.deg2rad(lat))[:, None] * np.ones((1, forecast.sizes["lon"]))
area_mean = mean(["lat", "lon"], weights=weights)
average = area_mean(forecast)

Match weight axes to the reduced dimensions in input-dimension order; use actual cell areas for other geometries. For ensemble forecasts, metrics such as rmse accept ensemble_dimension="ensemble" to compare the ensemble mean with observations; CRPS instead evaluates the predictive distribution.

To accumulate across time batches with consistent surviving coordinates:

running_mean = mean(["time"], batch_update=True)
for batch in batches:
    average_so_far = running_mean(batch)

Each result covers all batches seen by that instance. Create a new instance to start an independent stream.

docs.title: Create Your Own Statistic or Metric
docs.text: Implement the interface in a local module. Declare reductions and any added axes in output_coords without reading values; ensure execution returns exactly those coordinates. Validate metric input compatibility before arithmetic so Xarray's automatic alignment cannot silently change the comparison. If you support weights or streaming updates, document their shapes and lifetime. See the extension examples for custom components.

docs.title: Build Process
docs.text:
This page describes how to set the package version and build a wheel for Earth2Studio from a local clone. It is intended for contributors and maintainers.

Prerequisites: uv installed, a clone of the repository, and a synced development environment (for example, uv sync as described in the Developer Overview). Run all commands below from the repository root (the directory that contains pyproject.toml).

docs.title: Setting the Version
docs.text:
To check the version of the current package:

uv run hatch version

To bump the version automatically, use the following hatch commands:

# To bump to next pre-release
uv run hatch version minor,a

# To bump to release candidate version
uv run hatch version rc

# To bump to final release version
uv run hatch version release

docs.title: Building a Wheel
docs.text:
To build the wheel, use the uv build command:

uv build

docs.title: Dependency Management
docs.text: Earth2Studio uses uv as its primary package manager to handle complex dependency relationships between different models, data sources, and utilities. This choice helps maintain a clean, reproducible environment while avoiding dependency conflicts and bloat.

docs.title: Base Dependencies
docs.text:
The base installation provides core functionality that is focused on the relative ecosystem surrounding the following five packages:

  • torch: Deep learning framework
  • xarray: Multi-dimensional (N-D) labeled arrays and datasets
  • zarr: Array storage format
  • fsspec: Filesystem interfaces
  • obstore: Rust-based object storage client (S3/GCS/Azure) backing the Zarr data sources

With these base dependencies, most IO methods, data sources, perturbation methods, and utilities should be functional. However, specific features can require additional optional dependencies.

Adding Packages

uv commands should always be used to update package lists inside the pyproject.toml. Refer to the uv documentation for details about this if unfamiliar.

docs.title: Optional Dependencies
docs.text:
Earth2Studio uses uv's dependency groups to organize optional features:

# Example pyproject.toml structure
[project.optional-dependencies]
# Data
data = [
    "cdsapi>=0.7.5",
    "eccodes>=2.38.0",
    "ecmwf-opendata>=0.3.3",
    "herbie-data",
]
# PX Models
aurora = [
    "microsoft-aurora>=1.5.0",
]
aurora-fork = [
    "microsoft-aurora", # optional fork install without timm package version conflict
]
dlwp = [
    "nvidia-physicsnemo>=1.0.1",
]

Each model and major feature set has its own optional dependency group. This allows users to:

  1. Install only what they need
  2. Avoid potential conflicts between different models
  3. Keep the base installation lightweight

Earth2Studio also attempts to maintain a best effort "all" optional group that can be updated accordingly.

docs.title: Handling Optional Imports
docs.text:
When developing features that require optional dependencies, always use graceful error handling for the user to communicate if an additional dependency group needs to be installed. A good sanity check is to run make docs from the repository root to build the API documentation and verify that optional imports are handled correctly. For targets and setup, refer to building_documentation.

It is important to handle the absence of optional dependencies in a standardized way for the user. Earth2Studio has some utilities to provide informative errors to users that should be used when some optional dependency group is needed to be installed:

  1. Use a try or except around the optional import for ImportError. Set respective package objects to None if not installed. The file should not error on import; optional imports should be evaluated lazily when needed.
  2. In the catch of the import try catch, instantiate a OptionalDependencyFailure. The only parameter needed is the name of the dependency group that needs to be installed.
  3. Place the @check_optional_dependencies decorator on the class and/or function that requires the optional import. This will check to make sure that the required imports are installed when the user attempts to use the respective feature.

For example in the FourCastNet model:

from earth2studio.utils.imports import (
    OptionalDependencyFailure,
    check_optional_dependencies,
)
try:
    from physicsnemo.models.afno import AFNO
except ImportError:
    OptionalDependencyFailure("fcn")
    AFNO = None


# Use the decorator on classes
@check_optional_dependencies()
class FCN(torch.nn.Module, AutoModelMixin, PrognosticMixin):
    ...
    # Use the decorator on functions
    @classmethod
    @check_optional_dependencies()
    def load_model(
        cls,
        package: Package,
    ) -> PrognosticModel:

    ...

In this example, you can import the FCN module without errors. Only when you use FCN without the required extra packages installed will the following error appear:

docs.title: Managing Conflicts
docs.text:
Earth2Studio uses uv's conflict resolution system to explicitly handle package incompatibilities:

# Example conflict resolution in pyproject.toml
[tool.uv]
conflicts = [
    [
      { extra = "aurora" },
      { extra = "dlwp" },
    ],
]

All potential conflicts should be documented in the pyproject.toml file to ensure reproducible environments.

docs.title: Developer Dependencies
docs.text:
Development dependencies are managed separately using uv dependency groups:

# Example dependency group in pyproject.toml
[dependency-groups]
dev = [
    "black==24.1.0",
    "coverage>=6.5.0",
    "interrogate>=1.5.0",
    "hatch>=1.14.0",
    "mypy"
]

These dependencies are not included in the distributed package wheel. For more information on dependency management with uv, refer to the following:

  • uv Dependency Documentation
  • uv Conflict Resolution

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text: Earth2Studio builds its documentation with MkDocs and Material for MkDocs.

docs.title: Source layout
docs.text:
• docs/modules/: API landing pages consumed by docs/generate_api.py.
  • docs/userguide/: conceptual and developer guides.
  • examples/: executable gallery sources.
  • docs/examples/: generated gallery pages; do not edit these directly.

The docs generators also create the model catalog, installation options, and scorecard pages. earth2studio-gallery renders examples and retained execution results without Sphinx.

docs.title: Docstrings
docs.text:
Public classes and functions require docstrings; Interrogate enforces coverage. Use NumPy-style docstrings with these conventions:

  • Start the summary on the opening """ line.
  • Document classes on the class definition, not __init__.
  • Include argument and return types.
  • Mark optional arguments and state their defaults.
  • End complete sentences with periods.
def timearray_to_datetime(time: TimeArray) -> list[datetime]:
    """Convert a NumPy datetime64 array into Python datetimes.

    Parameters
    ----------
    time : TimeArray
        NumPy datetime64 array.

    Returns
    -------
    list[datetime]
        Converted datetime objects.
    """

docs.title: Local builds
docs.text:
• make docs: generate all pages and build from retained example results.
  • make docs-full: execute stale examples, regenerate the gallery, and build.
  • make docs-dev: serve locally with live reload.
  • make docs-dev FILENAME=<selector>: execute one example, then serve the complete gallery.

For example:

make docs-dev FILENAME=01_getting_started/01_deterministic_workflow.py

Build output is written to site/. Project-mode examples use the repository's pyproject.toml and uv.lock, syncing only their declared extras.

docs.title: CI builds
docs.text:
• Pull requests run make docs only. They do not execute examples, upload the site, write caches, or deploy.
  • Pushes to main run the cache-only docs workflow and deploy the site.
  • The manual full workflow publishes the cache-only site, runs all eight example sections sequentially, then publishes the site again with the updated Gallery results.

Each example section has its own data cache. Gallery results use one rolling cache passed between sections. Missing caches are valid cold starts; interrupted restores fail the job. Model downloads are not cached. The remaining sections continue after a section failure, but the final publish requires every section to succeed.

Use the util-clear-cache workflow to clear Gallery or docs-data caches.

docs.title: GitHub Pages
docs.text:
Keep docs/.nojekyll in the source tree. It allows GitHub Pages to serve generated directories such as _static/ and examples/_assets/.

Versioned deployments use Mike:

DOC_VERSION=0.18.0 make docs-deploy-version

Versions are published at https://nvidia.github.io/earth2studio/<version>/.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: This page describes how to set up a local development environment with uv, optional documentation dependencies, and pre-commit hooks. It assumes you have reviewed the repository and are familiar with the majority of the information found in the User Guide.

docs.title: Environment Setup
docs.text:
When developing Earth2Studio, using a uv virtual environment is suggested and will be used in the documentation. To create a local development environment with a git repo and uv:

  1. Clone the repo and use uv to create a Python 3.13 virtual environment and sync it with the dev dependency group:

    # Replace with your fork
git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA/earth2studio.git --single-branch

cd earth2studio

uv venv --python=3.13
uv sync # This will install the base and developer dependencies

    This should create a Python virtual environment inside of the local Earth2Studio git repository.

  2. To install the base, developer, documentation dependencies, use:

    uv sync --group docs

Note

When working with models, additional optional dependencies might be required. Refer to the Install Guide for details on the optional dependencies inside the package. Use the uv sync --extra <optional dep> command instead of pip install. Take note of the difference between the optional dependency groups used here and the extra dependencies when using specific models.

docs.title: Pre-commit
docs.text:
For Earth2Studio development, pre-commit is required. This will not only help developers pass the CI pipeline, but also accelerate reviews. Contributions that have not used pre-commit will not be reviewed.

To install pre-commit run the following inside the Earth2Studio repository folder:

uv pip install pre-commit
uv run pre-commit install

>>> pre-commit installed at .git/hooks/pre-commit

After the above commands are executed, the pre-commit hooks are activated and all the commits are checked for appropriate formatting, linting.

docs.title: Recipe Guide
docs.text:
Earth2Studio recipes are reference solutions that focus on solving specific use cases. Recipes provide more complex implementations that may require deeper domain knowledge and familiarity with the codebase.

Warning

Earth2Studio recipes are in beta and can change dramatically or be moved.

docs.title: What is a Recipe?
docs.text:
While examples demonstrate how to use features, recipes focus on how to solve specific problems. Recipes are not intended to be turnkey solutions with every potential option; rather, they are reference or boilerplate projects for different common use cases.

Here's how examples differ:

  • Self-contained Jupytext format
  • Focus on demonstrating specific features
  • Include graphical output for Sphinx Gallery
  • Required to be part of earth2studio + docs dep group
  • Single GPU, A100 (40G) max resource requirement
  • Run in less than 10 minutes

docs.title: Recipes
docs.text:
• Require multiple support files
  • Focus on providing complete solutions
  • Configuration YAMLs and JSONs
  • Pythonic interaction through main.py
  • Requirements provided in pyproject.toml
  • May require more specific hardware or system dependencies

Refer to Examples for more information on creating an example.

docs.title: Recipe Structure
docs.text:
The recipe template defines what a recipe should contain and look like, including folders, README sections, and support files. Recipes have the following structure:

recipes/
 |- recipe-name/
    cfg/
    |- config.yaml # Configuration files
    src/
    |- *.py # Support files
    test/
    |- test.py # Test files
    main.py # Main interaction script
    README.md # Recipe documentation
    recipe-requirements.txt # Exported requirements
    pyproject.toml # Project configuration

docs.title: Recipe Guidelines
docs.text:
1. Code Standards

    • Must follow all pre-commit standards and code practices.
    • Must include end-to-end tests validating functionality.
    • No images, data files, or other file formats are allowed in the repo; link to assets that are hosted externally instead. Earth2Studio has a HuggingFace assets dataset that can be used.
    • Implementation or re-implementation of components that exist in Earth2Studio package is not encouraged. Upstreaming is a priority.

  2. Testing

    • Should include end-to-end tests with expected results to verify functionality.
    • Not included in the main pytest suite.
    • Tested following major release cycles.

  3. Ownership

    • Must have designated owners (listed as authors in pyproject.toml).
    • Owners are responsible for fixing bugs and updates.
    • Recipes can and may be removed based on their use or relevance.

  4. Dependencies

    • Must use shipped versions of Earth2Studio (not the main branch).
    • Dependencies are managed through pyproject.toml using uv.
    • A requirements.txt should also be provided for pip install.

  5. Documentation

    • Clear README.md explaining purpose and usage.
    • Can include Jupytext notebooks for interactive documentation.
    • Should reference related examples when applicable.
    • Links to the recipes should be added to the recipe index.
    • Recipes can provide related plotting functionality.

docs.title: Creating a New Recipe
docs.text:
To create a new recipe, you can use the template provided in the recipes directory:

cp -r recipes/template recipes/my_new_recipe
cd recipes/my_new_recipe

Update the pyproject.toml to reflect the correct metadata:

[project]
name = "newrecipe"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "My New Recipe"
readme = "README.md"
requires-python = ">=3.10"
authors = [
  { name="My Name", email = "optional@example.com" },
]

Inside the recipe dependencies can be added or removed using uv. For example:

uv sync
uv add cartopy

# Update the recipe-requirements.txt
uv export --format requirements-txt --no-hashes >> recipe-requirements.txt

Because recipes are more extensive, expect a longer review timeline. Making iterative updates expanding functionality is preferred.

docs.title: AI Agent Skills
docs.text: Earth2Studio includes AI agent skills that provide specialized guidance for AI coding assistants (Claude Code, Codex, etc.) when working with Earth2Studio. These skills help agents build inference pipelines, select models, and generate correct code.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Skills are located in the skills/ directory at the repository root. Each skill contains:

  • SKILL.md - Instructions and workflow for the AI agent
  • evals/evals.json - Evaluation tasks for testing skill effectiveness
  • evals/targets/ - Reference outputs for evaluation grading
  • references/ - Supporting documentation (optional)

Note

Skill development is currently internal to NVIDIA. External contributions to skills are not accepted at this time.

docs.title: Skill Validation
docs.text:
Skills are validated using the harbor agent evaluation framework via nv-base. To run skill evaluations locally:

nv-base agent-eval <path-to-skill> -a claude-code,codex -r cli,html,json -o ./eval-results/

For example, to evaluate the deterministic forecast skill:

nv-base agent-eval skills/earth2studio-deterministic-forecast \
    -a claude-code,codex \
    -r cli,html,json \
    -o ./eval-results/

This produces:

  • cli - Console output with pass/fail summary
  • html - Interactive HTML report for detailed analysis
  • json - Machine-readable results for CI integration

docs.title: Evaluation Metrics
docs.text:
Skills are evaluated across five dimensions:

Dimension Description Security Avoids unsafe operations, secret leakage, unauthorized access Correctness Agent follows expected workflow and produces correct output Discoverability Agent loads skill when relevant, avoids when irrelevant Effectiveness Agent performs better with skill than without Efficiency Agent uses fewer tokens and avoids redundant work

docs.title: Style Guide
docs.text: The Earth2Studio style guide is a set of conventions we have adopted detailing how to write code for this project. A consistent style and process makes the package much easier to understand for users and ensures compliance requirements are met.

docs.title: Code Formatting
docs.text:
Earth2Studio uses black as the code formatter. All committed code is expected to be compliant with the version of black specified in the pyproject.toml. Pre-commit will format your code for you or you can run make format to run black on all files.

Additional code formatting principles:

  • File names are always lower case and use a shortened name for the component they contain
  • Class names are capitalized using Pascal case
  • Function names are lower case using snake case

docs.title: Linting
docs.text: Linting is performed by ruff, which includes many processes to ensure code between files is as consistent as possible. Ruff is configured in the project's pyproject.toml. Pre-commit will run linting for you or you can run make lint to run ruff on all files.

docs.title: Type Hints
docs.text:
Earth2Studio is a MyPy compliant package, meaning type hints are required for all functions (parameters and return type). MyPy is configured in the package's pyproject.toml. On top of requiring type hints, the following guidelines should be used:

  • To help keep APIs concise, several of the common types used throughout the package are defined in earth2studio/utils/type.py, which should be used when applicable.
from collections import OrderedDict
from datetime import timedelta

import numpy as np
import xarray as xr

FrameSchema = OrderedDict[str, np.ndarray]
CoordSystem = OrderedDict[str, np.ndarray]
CoordinateSystem = xr.DataArray

# Specific dimension custom types
VariableArray = np.ndarray[str]
LeadTimeArray = np.ndarray[np.timedelta64]
TimeArray = np.ndarray[np.datetime64]
MemberArray = np.ndarray
FieldArray = np.ndarray[str]

TimeTolerance = (
    timedelta
    | np.timedelta64
    | tuple[timedelta, timedelta]
    | tuple[np.timedelta64, np.timedelta64]
)

  • Earth2Studio is Python 3.10+, thus type hinting using generic objects should be used instead of the typing package. Refer to PEP 585 for details.

  • Earth2Studio is Python 3.10+, thus the | operator should be used instead of Union and Optional type operators. Refer to PEP 604 for details.

Note

The pre-commit hook PyUpgrade will enforce Python 3.10 type styles automatically.

docs.title: Signing Your Work

To sign off on a commit, use the --signoff (or -s) option when committing your changes:

git commit -s -m "Adding a cool feature."

This will append the following to your commit message:
